talk_about: Why is it useful for lions to live in a family instead of alone?
If you could hear something 5 miles away, what would you listen for?
Which other animal at the zoo lives in a family group?
push_further: A mane makes a male slower, hotter and more visible. Why hasn’t evolution removed it?
Lions and cheetahs share the same plains. How do they avoid competing directly?
Find one more animal on your zoo map that lives in a group. What does the group give it?

teach: A group of lions is a pride.
A baby is a cub.
They live on grasslands / savannah, not jungle.
Their famous sound is a roar.
Male lions often grow a big mane.

questions.title: Family
questions.stem: What do you call a group of lions?
choices: A pride
A pack
A herd
questions.why: Lions live together in a pride — a social group that shares space and raises cubs.

questions.title: Food
questions.stem: What do lions mostly eat?
choices: Grass
Meat
Fruit
questions.why: Lions eat meat. They mostly hunt hooved animals such as zebra, wildebeest, and antelope.

questions.title: Voice
questions.stem: What sound is a lion famous for?
choices: A moo
A squeak
A roar
questions.why: A lion’s roar can travel a long way — about 8 km / 5 miles (Wikipedia).

questions.title: Mane
questions.stem: Which lion usually grows a big fluffy mane?
choices: The male
The female
Both
questions.why: Male lions often grow a big mane around the head and neck.

questions.title: Young
questions.stem: What is a baby lion called?
choices: A calf
A cub
A chick
questions.why: A baby lion is a cub. Many cubs have faint spots that fade as they grow.

questions.title: Home
questions.stem: Where do wild lions mostly live?
choices: Thick jungle
Deep ocean
Grassland / savannah
questions.why: Wild lions mostly live on grassland, savannah, and shrubland — rarely in closed forest.

questions.title: Rest
questions.stem: How much of the day do lions often spend resting?
choices: About 20 hours
About 2 hours
About 8 hours
questions.why: Lions often rest or stay inactive for about 20 hours a day.

questions.title: Hunting
questions.stem: In a pride, who usually does most of the hunting?
choices: The dads
The moms (lionesses)
The cubs
questions.why: In a pride, lionesses usually do most of the hunting, often together.

questions.title: Tail
questions.stem: What special tip does a lion’s tail have?
choices: Feathers
A shell
A dark hairy tuft
questions.why: A lion’s tail ends in a dark hairy tuft.

questions.title: Myth buster
questions.stem: Do lions really live in a jungle like in some cartoons?
choices: No — mostly open grassland
Yes, always
Only in snow
questions.why: Cartoons show jungle lions, but wild lions mostly live on open grassland.

questions.title: Name
questions.stem: What is the lion’s scientific name?
choices: Panthera leo
Felis catus
Canis lupus
questions.why: The lion is a large cat in the genus Panthera. Its scientific name is Panthera leo.

questions.title: Pride
questions.stem: In a typical pride, who forms the stable core?
choices: A pack of unrelated males
Related females and their cubs
Only cubs with no adults
questions.why: A pride’s stable core is related females and cubs. Adult males are usually unrelated to those females.

questions.title: Prey
questions.stem: What do wild lions mostly hunt?
choices: Tiny prey like hares and monkeys
Only fish
Medium and large hooved mammals
questions.why: Lions mostly hunt medium-sized and large hooved mammals such as zebra, wildebeest, and buffalo — not tiny prey as their main diet.

questions.title: Speed
questions.stem: How do lions usually chase prey?
choices: Short fast bursts of about 30–37 mph
Long stamina runs for many miles
They never run
questions.why: Lions have quick burst speed of about 48–59 km/h (30–37 mph) but little stamina, so they do not run long chases.

questions.title: Status snapshot
questions.stem: How does the IUCN list wild lions today?
choices: Least Concern — a forever safe grade
Often listed Vulnerable — a snapshot that can be revised
Extinct in the wild
questions.why: Lions have often been listed as Vulnerable, and African populations have declined sharply. Habitat loss and conflict with people are key worries. Status letters can change when new counts arrive, so we treat Vulnerable as a snapshot, not a forever grade.

questions.title: Range
questions.stem: Where do wild Asiatic lions live today?
choices: All across Asia
Only in zoos
Mainly Gir National Park in western India
questions.why: Wild Asiatic lions today survive mainly in and around Gir National Park in Gujarat, western India.

questions.title: Cubs
questions.stem: When can a newborn lion cub see?
choices: Eyes open around a week after birth
It is born with eyes already open
Eyes stay closed for a year
questions.why: Lion cubs are born blind. Their eyes open around seven days after birth.

questions.title: Birth
questions.stem: About how long is a lioness’s pregnancy, and how many cubs are usual?
choices: About 30 days; often 12 cubs
About 110 days; often 1–4 cubs
About two years; one cub only
questions.why: Gestation is about 110 days. A litter is often between one and four cubs.

questions.title: Takeover
questions.stem: What often happens to young cubs when new males take over a pride?
choices: The new males adopt every cub
Cubs immediately leave to hunt alone
The new males often kill existing young cubs
questions.why: When new males oust the previous males, they often kill existing young cubs. Females then become ready to mate sooner.

questions.title: Color
questions.stem: What makes a white lion white?
choices: A rare pale morph from leucism, with normal eye and skin pigment
It is a true albino with pink eyes
It is painted by keepers
questions.why: White lions are a rare pale morph caused by leucism, not true albinism. They still have normal pigmentation in the eyes and skin.

questions.title: Roar
questions.stem: What helps a lion roar, unlike a house cat’s continuous purr?
choices: A stretchy hyoid ligament (not a fully stiff bone)
A fully stiff hyoid bone like a house cat
Hollow horns that amplify sound
questions.why: One reason lions can roar is a stretchy hyoid ligament in the throat — not a fully stiff bone like a house cat. They do not make a house cat’s continuous purr.

questions.title: Scent
questions.stem: When a lion curls its lips in a flehmen grimace, where does the scent go?
choices: Straight into the lungs only
Toward the vomeronasal organ
Into the ear canal
questions.why: The flehmen face (open mouth, wrinkled nose) helps a lion sniff chemical signals. The lip-curl routes scent toward the vomeronasal organ, a special smell sensor.

questions.title: Teeth
questions.stem: What are a lion’s carnassial teeth built to do?
choices: Grind grass like a cow
Hold water
Shear meat with blade-like cheek teeth (upper P4 / lower m1)
questions.why: Carnassials are blade-like cheek teeth — the upper fourth premolar and lower first molar — that shear meat.

questions.title: Species
questions.stem: Which two living lion subspecies do scientists recognize today?
choices: Panthera leo leo and Panthera leo melanochaita
Cave lion and American lion
Only the Barbary lion
questions.why: In 2017 the Cat Specialist Group recognized two living subspecies: P. l. leo and P. l. melanochaita. Cave lions and American lions are extinct relatives, not living subspecies.

questions.title: Tail
questions.stem: What can hide inside a lion’s dark tail tuft?
choices: A venom stinger
A small hard spur; its function is unknown
A second claw used for climbing
questions.why: In some lions the dark tail tuft hides a small hard spur. Wikipedia notes its function is unknown.

questions.title: Takeover
questions.stem: Why do new males often kill young cubs after taking over a pride?
choices: To teach cubs to hunt
Because cubs eat only plants
So females return to estrus and can mate sooner
questions.why: Females usually do not become ready to mate again until their cubs grow up or die. Killing young cubs often brings females back into estrus sooner.

questions.title: Society
questions.stem: How do lions compare with other wild cats?
choices: They are the most social of wild cats, living in prides
They are the only cats that never meet
They are less social than typical solitary big cats
questions.why: The lion is the most social of all wild felid species. Related females and cubs form a pride — unlike typical solitary big cats.

questions.title: Decline
questions.stem: What are the greatest causes for concern in the lion’s decline?
choices: Too much rain only
Habitat loss and conflict with people
Lions moving to the deep ocean
questions.why: The exact drop is not fully understood, but habitat loss and conflicts with people are the greatest concerns. IUCN has listed lions Vulnerable — we treat that letter as a snapshot, not a forever grade.

questions.title: Muscle
questions.stem: Why do lions hunt with short rushes instead of long chases?
choices: They have no leg muscles
They prefer to fly
They have a high share of fast-twitch muscle and little stamina
questions.why: Lion muscle has a high concentration of fast-twitch fibers, so they can sprint in short bursts but have little stamina.

questions.title: Rivals
questions.stem: How do lions and spotted hyenas treat each other’s kills?
choices: They steal kills from each other (kleptoparasitism both ways)
They never notice each other
Hyenas only eat plants
questions.why: Lions and spotted hyenas compete for prey and carrion. Each species may steal the other’s kills — kleptoparasitism goes both ways.

reticulated-giraffe.source_note: Facts from Wikipedia, Giraffe / Reticulated giraffe.
talk_about: Why might a long neck help a giraffe besides reaching high leaves?
If you stood as tall as a giraffe, what would you notice first at the zoo?
Which other animal at the zoo has a special tongue or a long neck?
push_further: A giraffe must spread its front legs to drink. What risk could that pose in the wild?
Each giraffe’s spots are unique. How could that help a keeper tell them apart?
Find one more animal on your zoo map that eats leaves from trees. How does it reach them?

teach: The giraffe is the tallest living land animal.
It eats leaves and shoots from tall trees.
A very long neck helps it reach high foliage.
A baby giraffe is a calf.
Wild giraffes live on African savannah and open woodland.

questions.title: Tallest
questions.stem: What record does a giraffe hold among living land animals?
choices: Tallest living land animal
Fastest runner
Smallest mammal
questions.why: The giraffe is the tallest living land animal — taller than any other animal that lives on land today.

questions.title: Food
questions.stem: What do giraffes mostly eat?
choices: Meat
Leaves and shoots from tall trees
Fish
questions.why: Giraffes eat leaves and shoots from tall trees, especially acacia. They are not meat-eaters.

questions.title: Neck
questions.stem: Why does a giraffe have such a long neck?
choices: To store water like a camel
To fly
To reach high leaves
questions.why: A giraffe’s extremely long neck helps it reach high foliage that shorter animals cannot.

questions.title: Tongue
questions.stem: What is special about a giraffe’s tongue?
choices: It is very long and dark, for stripping leaves
It is forked like a snake
It is short and used only to drink
questions.why: A giraffe uses a very long, dark tongue to pull and strip leaves from thorny branches.

questions.title: Young
questions.stem: What is a baby giraffe called, and what can it do soon after birth?
choices: A cub — it stays lying down for weeks
A calf — it can stand soon after birth
A chick — it hatches from an egg
questions.why: A baby giraffe is a calf. Newborns can stand soon after they are born.

questions.title: Home
questions.stem: Where do wild giraffes mostly live?
choices: Deep ocean
Thick polar ice
African savannah and open woodland
questions.why: Wild giraffes live on African savannah and open woodland — not only one country.

questions.title: Drink
questions.stem: How does a giraffe drink water?
choices: It spreads its front legs or bends its knees
It uses a trunk
It never drinks water
questions.why: A giraffe’s neck and legs are so long that it spreads its front legs or bends its knees to reach the water.

questions.title: Ossicones
questions.stem: What are the horn-like bumps on a giraffe’s head?
choices: Antlers that fall off each year
Skin-covered ossicones
Ears that folded up
questions.why: Those bumps are ossicones — skin-covered, horn-like knobs. They are not antlers that shed.

questions.title: Coat
questions.stem: What is special about a giraffe’s coat?
choices: Every giraffe has the same spots
It is bright blue with stripes
Dark patches in a net-like pattern; each giraffe’s spots are unique
questions.why: A reticulated giraffe’s dark patches look like a net. Each giraffe’s spot pattern is unique.

questions.title: Myth buster
questions.stem: Does a giraffe have extra neck bones compared with most mammals?
choices: No — still seven vertebrae, just much longer
Yes — dozens of extra bones
It has no neck bones
questions.why: Like most mammals, a giraffe has seven neck vertebrae. Each bone is just much longer.

questions.title: Relatives
questions.stem: What is the giraffe’s closest living relative?
choices: The okapi (both are Giraffidae)
The camel
The elephant
questions.why: Giraffes and the okapi are the only living members of family Giraffidae. The okapi is the giraffe’s closest living relative.

questions.title: Name
questions.stem: What does the old English name “camelopard” mean?
choices: A desert camel only
Camel-like shape plus leopard-like spots
A spotted leopard from Asia
questions.why: “Camelopard” comes from Greek words for camel and leopard — a camel-like shape with leopard-like colouration.

questions.title: Ossicones
questions.stem: What are a giraffe’s ossicones made of?
choices: Antlers that shed each year
Hollow horns that fall off
Ossified cartilage covered in skin and fused to the skull
questions.why: Ossicones form from ossified cartilage, stay covered in skin, and fuse to the skull. They are not antlers that shed.

questions.title: Necking
questions.stem: How do male giraffes usually fight to establish dominance?
choices: They swing their necks and land blows with ossicones
They roar at each other
They lock antlers and push
questions.why: Males “neck” — swinging their necks and trying to land blows with their ossicones to decide who is dominant.

questions.title: Speed
questions.stem: How fast can a giraffe gallop in a short burst?
choices: It cannot run at all
Roughly 30–37 mph in short bursts
Faster than a cheetah for hours
questions.why: Giraffes can gallop roughly 30–37 mph in short bursts. They are not built for long, all-day chases.

questions.title: Ruminate
questions.stem: How does a giraffe chew its food a second time?
choices: It never chews again after the first swallow
It stores food in its ossicones
It has a four-chambered stomach and brings cud back up the long neck
questions.why: Giraffes are ruminants with a four-chambered stomach. Strong oesophageal muscles send cud back up the long neck to be chewed again.

questions.title: Sleep
questions.stem: How do giraffes usually sleep?
choices: In short bouts that add up to only a few hours a day
They sleep about 20 hours a day like lions
They never sleep
questions.why: Giraffes sleep in short, interrupted bouts that total only a few hours a day — not one long night of sleep.

questions.title: Calves
questions.stem: How tall is a newborn giraffe, and how soon can it run?
choices: Mouse-sized; it cannot walk for months
Already about as tall as a person, and it can run within hours
Taller than an adult giraffe on day one
questions.why: A newborn calf is already about as tall as a person. Within a few hours it can run, though it still hides a lot in the first weeks.

questions.title: Threats
questions.stem: What are the main threats to wild giraffes today?
choices: Too much rain only
Giraffes moving to the deep ocean
Habitat loss and hunting for bushmeat
questions.why: The biggest concerns are habitat loss and killing for bushmeat. Exact IUCN labels have shifted as giraffe species were split.

questions.title: Tongue
questions.stem: Why might a giraffe’s tongue be dark?
choices: The dark colour may help protect it from sunburn while browsing
To taste only meat
To scare other giraffes
questions.why: A giraffe’s tongue is dark — Wikipedia notes it is black, perhaps to protect against sunburn while the animal browses in the sun.

questions.title: Species
questions.stem: How do many scientists treat living giraffes today?
choices: Often as several species (often four); the reticulated giraffe is Giraffa reticulata
Always one species forever, with no debate
Only as two extinct fossil species
questions.why: Giraffes were long treated as one species. Many researchers now recognize several living species — often four — and the reticulated giraffe as Giraffa reticulata. Wikipedia treats that recognition as ongoing debate, not a forever rule.

questions.title: Heart
questions.stem: Why must a giraffe’s heart work so hard to supply the brain?
choices: The heart is tiny and barely beats
It must generate roughly double typical human blood pressure to push blood up the long neck
Giraffes have no blood vessels in the neck
questions.why: Wikipedia says the giraffe heart must generate about double the blood pressure a human needs to keep blood flowing to the brain. Exact pressure readings vary, so we keep the “roughly double” idea.

questions.title: Circulation
questions.stem: What helps protect a giraffe’s brain when the head drops to drink?
choices: Extra lungs in the ossicones
The tongue plugs the windpipe
A rete mirabile in the neck plus valves in the jugular veins
questions.why: When the head lowers, a rete mirabile — a net of vessels in the upper neck — plus valves in the jugular veins keep too much blood from flooding the brain.

questions.title: Neck bones
questions.stem: How is a giraffe’s neck built, compared with most other mammals?
choices: It still has seven cervical vertebrae, each greatly lengthened
It added many extra cervical vertebrae
The neck is one solid bone with no joints
questions.why: Like most mammals, a giraffe still has seven cervical vertebrae. Each bone is greatly lengthened — the neck did not gain a stack of extra bones.

questions.title: Scent
questions.stem: How do male giraffes check whether a female is ready to mate?
choices: They listen for a roar
They taste her urine (flehmen), sending cues toward the vomeronasal organ
They count her spots
questions.why: Males use the flehmen response: tasting a female’s urine to detect oestrus. The lip-curl routes chemical cues toward the vomeronasal organ.

questions.title: Gestation
questions.stem: About how long is giraffe pregnancy, and how many calves are usual?
choices: About two weeks; often a dozen calves
About 30 days; twins every time
Roughly 400–460 days; usually one calf
questions.why: Wikipedia gives gestation as about 400–460 days. Usually one calf is born; twins are rare. We keep that range rather than one exact day count.

questions.title: Evolution
questions.stem: What two main ideas does Wikipedia discuss for why giraffe necks became so long?
choices: Competing browsers reaching high food, and sexual selection via necking
Only swimming, with no other idea
Necks grew so giraffes could hibernate
questions.why: Wikipedia discusses both the competing-browsers idea (reaching food others cannot) and sexual selection (long necks helping males in necking contests). Scientists still debate which mattered more.

questions.title: Spots
questions.stem: What may the skin under a giraffe’s dark patches do besides camouflage?
choices: Store extra water like a camel hump
Hold complex blood vessels and large sweat glands that may help cool the body
Make electricity
questions.why: Wikipedia notes the skin under the dark blotches has complex blood-vessel systems and large sweat glands, which may help the giraffe regulate body temperature.

questions.title: Nerves
questions.stem: What is striking about a giraffe’s left recurrent laryngeal nerve?
choices: It is the shortest nerve in any mammal
It only exists in baby giraffes
It takes an extreme detour down the neck and back up, making it extraordinarily long
questions.why: In mammals the left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around a vessel near the heart, then returns to the larynx. In a giraffe that detour is extraordinarily long — a classic comparative-anatomy example.

questions.title: Society
questions.stem: How do giraffe social groups actually work?
choices: Fission–fusion groups, with lasting female associations and kinship
Purely random open herds with no lasting ties
Only solitary animals that never meet
questions.why: Giraffe groups were once called open and ever-changing. Newer work describes a fission–fusion society: groups split and join, but females often keep lasting associations and kinship ties.

african-elephant.source_note: Facts from Wikipedia, African elephant / Elephant.
talk_about: Why might a trunk be more useful than hands at the zoo?
If you had ears as big as an elephant’s, how would you stay cool?
Which other animal at the zoo lives in a family group?
push_further: An elephant’s trunk can grab, drink, and smell. What job would you give it first?
A herd follows the oldest female. Why might the oldest be a good leader?
Find one more big animal on your zoo map. How does it move if it cannot jump?

teach: The African elephant is the largest living land animal.
It eats plants — grass, leaves, and bark — not meat.
Its trunk can grab, drink, spray, and smell.
A baby elephant is a calf.
A herd is led by the oldest female.

questions.title: Biggest
questions.stem: What record does an African elephant hold among living land animals?
choices: Largest / heaviest living land animal
Tallest living land animal
Fastest runner
questions.why: The African elephant is the largest and heaviest living land animal.

questions.title: Food
questions.stem: What do African elephants eat?
choices: Meat
Plants — grass, leaves, and bark
Fish
questions.why: African elephants are herbivores. They eat plants such as grass, leaves, and bark — not meat.

questions.title: Trunk
questions.stem: What does an elephant use its trunk for?
choices: Only to hear
To fly
To grab, drink, spray, and smell
questions.why: The trunk is a long nose and upper lip. Elephants use it to grab food, drink, spray water, and smell.

questions.title: Ears
questions.stem: Why does an African elephant have such big ears?
choices: To stay cool
To fly
To store food
questions.why: Big ears help an African elephant shed heat and stay cool.

questions.title: Young
questions.stem: What is a baby elephant called?
choices: A cub
A calf
A chick
questions.why: A baby elephant is a calf. Calves stay close to mom and the rest of the family herd as they grow.

questions.title: Family
questions.stem: Who usually leads an elephant herd?
choices: The youngest calf
A lone zebra
The oldest female (the matriarch)
questions.why: Elephant families live in a herd led by the oldest female, called the matriarch.

questions.title: Tusks
questions.stem: What are an elephant’s tusks?
choices: Very long teeth
Horns made of hair
Feathers
questions.why: Tusks are very long teeth — not horns. Elephants use them to dig, lift, and strip bark.

questions.title: Voice
questions.stem: What sound is an elephant famous for?
choices: A moo
A trumpet
A meow
questions.why: An elephant’s famous call is a trumpet — a loud sound made through the trunk.

questions.title: Water
questions.stem: How can an African elephant swim?
choices: It cannot swim
It uses wings
It can swim, and its trunk can act like a snorkel
questions.why: Elephants can swim. They sometimes swim underwater and use the trunk like a snorkel.

questions.title: Myth buster
questions.stem: Can an elephant jump?
choices: No — elephants cannot jump
Yes — they hop like kangaroos
Only over tiny puddles
questions.why: Elephants cannot jump. Their heavy bodies stay on the ground.

questions.title: Trunk
questions.stem: How is an elephant’s trunk built, muscle-wise?
choices: Tens of thousands of muscles and no bone
One long bone down the middle
A hollow tube of cartilage only
questions.why: The trunk is a muscular hydrostat — tens of thousands of muscles and no bone. Published counts vary, so we do not lock one exact number.

questions.title: Voice
questions.stem: How do elephants often talk across long distances?
choices: Only by slapping their ears
With low-frequency rumbles, many too low for humans to hear
By flashing bright colours
questions.why: Elephants use infrasonic rumbles. Much of that communication is too low for humans, and it can travel far across the landscape.

questions.title: Gestation
questions.stem: About how long is African elephant pregnancy?
choices: About two weeks
About 22 years
About 22 months — the longest of any land mammal
questions.why: Calves are usually born after about 22 months. That is the longest pregnancy of any land mammal.

questions.title: Memory
questions.stem: Why can an older matriarch be especially important in a drought?
choices: Her memory of water and food can guide the family
She is the fastest runner
She stores water in her tusks
questions.why: The oldest female leads the herd. Her long memory of where water and food were in hard years can help the family survive drought.

questions.title: Teeth
questions.stem: How do elephants replace worn chewing teeth?
choices: They never get new teeth
New molars move forward from the back, like a conveyor, several times in a lifetime
They grow a new set all at once each year
questions.why: Worn front molars drop out as new ones move forward from the back. Elephants replace these chewing teeth several times in a lifetime.

questions.title: Feet
questions.stem: Why can such a heavy animal walk so quietly?
choices: It has feathers on its feet
It walks only on its toenails
Fatty cushion pads under the feet help nearly silent steps
questions.why: Soft fatty cushion pads under the feet spread the weight and help an elephant walk with almost no sound.

questions.title: Smell
questions.stem: How strong is an elephant’s sense of smell?
choices: Among the best senses of smell of any mammal
Elephants cannot smell at all
Only as strong as a goldfish
questions.why: An elephant’s trunk is a powerful nose. Elephants rank among the mammals with the best sense of smell.

questions.title: Threats
questions.stem: What are the main threats to wild African elephants today?
choices: Too many leaves
Ivory poaching and habitat loss
Elephants moving to the deep ocean
questions.why: The biggest threats are poaching for ivory and the loss and breakup of habitat.

questions.title: Compare
questions.stem: How can you usually tell an African elephant from an Asian elephant?
choices: African elephants have smaller ears and a rounded back
African elephants have no trunks
African elephants have larger ears and a concave (dipped) back
questions.why: African elephants typically have larger ears and a concave, dipped back. Asian elephants have smaller ears and a convex or level back.

questions.title: Myth buster
questions.stem: Are elephants really afraid of mice?
choices: No — that is a myth; they react to sudden movement, not mice specifically
Yes — they run from every mouse they see
Only pink mice
questions.why: “Afraid of mice” is a cartoon myth. Elephants may startle at sudden movement near their feet, not at mice as a special fear.

questions.title: Species
questions.stem: How do scientists treat living African elephants today?
choices: As two living species: bush/savanna Loxodonta africana and forest L. cyclotis
Always one species forever, with no split
Only as extinct mammoths
questions.why: Wikipedia treats living African elephants as two species — the bush or savanna elephant Loxodonta africana and the forest elephant L. cyclotis. IUCN assesses them separately. Status labels have shifted, so we do not lock one letter.

questions.title: Trunk
questions.stem: What is an elephant’s trunk, anatomically?
choices: A hollow bone like a horn
A fusion of the nose and the upper lip
Only a stretched nose, with no lip involved
questions.why: The trunk, or proboscis, is a prehensile elongation of the nose and upper lip. Those parts fuse in early development — it is not a nose alone.

questions.title: Trunk tip
questions.stem: How does an African elephant’s trunk tip differ from an Asian elephant’s?
choices: African elephants have no finger-like tip
Both have exactly five fingers
African elephants have two finger-like processes; Asian elephants have one
questions.why: African elephants have two finger-like processes at the tip of the trunk. Asian elephants have one and more often wrap the trunk around food.

questions.title: Senses
questions.stem: How can elephants pick up distant seismic signals?
choices: They detect ground-borne vibrations through their feet and trunk
Only by watching the sky
By tasting the air with their tusks
questions.why: Wikipedia notes elephants communicate with seismic vibrations that travel through the ground. They detect those ground-borne waves through the feet and the trunk.

questions.title: Musth
questions.stem: What happens when an adult bull elephant is in musth?
choices: He sheds his trunk
Testosterone rises; he becomes more aggressive and sexually active, with temporal-gland signs
He stops eating plants
questions.why: Musth is a state in adult males: elevated testosterone, heightened aggression and sexual activity, plus temporal-gland secretions running down the face.

questions.title: Family
questions.stem: Who besides the mother often helps care for an elephant calf?
choices: Only adult bulls
Passing zebras
Other young females in the family — allomothers
questions.why: Calves are cared for by their mother and other young females in the group, a pattern called allomothering or alloparenting.

questions.title: Teeth
questions.stem: What can happen after an old elephant’s last molar set wears out?
choices: The elephant may starve, because it can no longer grind plants well
New tusks become chewing teeth
It grows a bird-like beak
questions.why: After the final molar set wears out, an old elephant may starve — a common late-life cause of death. The last replacement is the last.

questions.title: Digestion
questions.stem: How do African elephants digest tough plants?
choices: With a four-chamber ruminant stomach like a giraffe
By hindgut fermentation
By storing food in the tusks
questions.why: Fermentation of food takes place in the hindgut. Elephants are hindgut fermenters, not four-chamber ruminants like giraffes.

questions.title: Genes
questions.stem: What gene story is linked to elephants’ size and cancer resistance?
choices: They have no tumor-suppressor genes
They rely on extra hearts only
They carry many copies of TP53, a gene linked to cancer resistance (Peto’s paradox)
questions.why: Elephants carry many copies of the TP53 tumor-suppressor gene, which researchers link to unusually low cancer rates for such large, long-lived animals — Peto’s paradox. Published copy counts vary, so we do not lock one number.

questions.title: Seeds
questions.stem: Why are African elephants sometimes called megagardeners?
choices: They are long-distance seed dispersers; dung can carry many plant species
They plant seeds with their tusks on purpose
They only eat meat and never spread seeds
questions.why: Elephants are long-distance seed dispersers. Seeds pass through the gut and germinate in dung, which can carry many plant species — a megagardener role in the landscape.

talk_about: Why might living in a colony help a penguin?
If you could “fly” underwater with flippers, what would you look for?
Which other animal at the zoo lives near the water?
push_further: A penguin’s coat is dark on top and pale below. How could that hide it from hunters?
African penguins nest on warm shores, not ice. Why might people think all penguins live somewhere cold?
Find one more bird on your zoo map that swims. How does it move in the water?

teach: African penguins live in Africa, not Antarctica.
They cannot fly in the air — they swim with flippers.
They eat fish and other sea food.
They live together in a colony.
They lay eggs in burrows or under bushes on the shore.

questions.title: Home
questions.stem: Where do wild African penguins live?
choices: Southern African coasts
Antarctica only
The North Pole
questions.why: African penguins live along southern African coasts, such as South Africa and Namibia — not Antarctica.

questions.title: Flight
questions.stem: Can an African penguin fly in the air?
choices: Yes — they fly like eagles
No — they are flightless and “fly” underwater with flippers
Only at night
questions.why: Like all penguins, African penguins cannot fly in the air. Their wings are stiff flippers they use to swim.

questions.title: Food
questions.stem: What do African penguins mostly eat?
choices: Grass and leaves
Bamboo
Fish and other sea prey, such as squid
questions.why: They hunt in the sea. Wikipedia says they feed primarily on fish and squid, plus other small sea animals.

questions.title: Voice
questions.stem: Why is the African penguin sometimes called a “jackass penguin”?
choices: It makes a loud, donkey-like bray
It looks like a donkey
It lives on a farm
questions.why: One nickname is “jackass penguin,” from the species’ loud, donkey-like call.

questions.title: Colony
questions.stem: What do you call a large group of African penguins living together?
choices: A pride
A colony
A herd
questions.why: African penguins live and breed together in a large group called a colony.

questions.title: Eggs
questions.stem: How do African penguins have babies?
choices: They give birth to live pups
They plant seeds
They lay eggs
questions.why: African penguins lay eggs. They do not give birth to live young.

questions.title: Coat
questions.stem: How does an African penguin’s black-and-white coat help it hide?
choices: Countershading — a dark back and pale belly hide it from hunters above and below
It makes the penguin glow in the dark
It keeps the penguin dry only
questions.why: The dark back blends with the water from above, and the pale belly is harder to see from below. That hiding trick is called countershading.

questions.title: Flippers
questions.stem: What are an African penguin’s wings like?
choices: Soft wings for flying in the air
Stiff, flat flippers for swimming
Long arms for climbing trees
questions.why: The wings are stiffened and flattened into flippers, made for swimming — not for flying in the air.

questions.title: Nest
questions.stem: Where do African penguins usually nest?
choices: On Antarctic ice
High in rainforest trees
In burrows or under bushes on the shore
questions.why: They nest in burrows or under rocks and bushes on the shore — not on ice.

questions.title: Myth buster
questions.stem: Do all penguins live on cold ice?
choices: No — African penguins live on warmer African coasts
Yes — every penguin lives on ice
Only in zoos
questions.why: Not every penguin lives somewhere icy. African penguins live on warmer coasts in southern Africa.

questions.title: Heat patch
questions.stem: What does the bare pink skin above an African penguin’s eye help it do?
choices: Lose heat — the patch flushes pinker when the bird is warmer
Hear better underwater
Store extra fish oil
questions.why: Bare pink skin above the eye helps dump heat. More blood flows there when the bird is warmer, so the patch looks pinker.

questions.title: Chest spots
questions.stem: What is special about an African penguin’s chest spots?
choices: Every penguin has the same spots
Each bird’s spot pattern is unique, like a fingerprint
The spots wash off in salt water
questions.why: The black spots on the chest form a pattern unique to each bird, like a human fingerprint. Keepers can use that to tell individuals apart.

questions.title: Moult
questions.stem: What happens in an African penguin’s catastrophic moult?
choices: It sheds a few feathers a day and keeps swimming
It never replaces its feathers
It sheds all its feathers at once and must stay out of the water for weeks while new ones grow
questions.why: Penguins moult all feathers at once. New feathers are not waterproof yet, so the bird stays on land and fasts for weeks while the coat grows back.

questions.title: Salt gland
questions.stem: How does an African penguin get rid of extra salt from seawater and sea food?
choices: A salt gland near the eye helps dump the extra salt
It never eats or drinks anything salty
It stores salt in its flippers
questions.why: A salt gland near the eye lets the penguin get rid of extra salt from seawater and a marine diet, so the body can stay in balance.

questions.title: Threats
questions.stem: What is the biggest problem facing wild African penguins today?
choices: Too many icebergs
Not enough prey fish, after commercial fishing and warming seas
Too many trees on the beach
questions.why: The biggest squeeze today is not enough prey fish. Commercial fishing and warming seas have made sardines and anchovies harder to find near colonies.

questions.title: Guano
questions.stem: How did old guano harvesting hurt African penguin nests?
choices: It painted the rocks bright white
It made the fish taste better
It removed the dung layer they dug nest burrows into
questions.why: Penguins once dug nest burrows into a thick guano (dung) layer. People harvested that dung for fertilizer, so many colonies lost the layer they nested in.

questions.title: Pairs
questions.stem: How do African penguin pairs often behave from year to year?
choices: They are often long-term and return to the same nest site
They pick a new partner every week
They never come back to land
questions.why: Pairs are often long-term. They tend to return to the same nest site each breeding season.

questions.title: Range
questions.stem: Where do African penguins breed in the wild?
choices: On Arctic ice with polar bears
On coasts and islands of southern Africa
Only in inland deserts
questions.why: They breed on coasts and islands of southern Africa, such as Namibia and South Africa — the only penguin that breeds on the African continent.

questions.title: Banded look
questions.stem: Why are African penguins called banded penguins?
choices: They wear metal ID bands only
They have rainbow stripes on their flippers
They belong to the Spheniscus group, with distinctive dark band(s) across the chest
questions.why: African penguins are banded (Spheniscus) penguins. They have distinctive dark band(s) across the chest — a light family look shared with a few other penguins.

questions.title: Myth buster
questions.stem: Do wild penguins and polar bears ever meet?
choices: No — they live at opposite ends of the planet
Yes — they share the same ice
Only in winter
questions.why: Polar bears live in the Arctic. Wild penguins live in the Southern Hemisphere. They never meet in the wild — opposite ends of the planet.

questions.title: Genus
questions.stem: Which genus do African penguins belong to, and who are their closest banded-penguin relatives?
choices: Spheniscus, with Humboldt, Magellanic, and Galápagos penguins
Aptenodytes, with emperor and king penguins
Pygoscelis, with Adélie, chinstrap, and gentoo penguins
questions.why: African penguins sit in Spheniscus, the banded penguins. Wikipedia groups them with Humboldt, Magellanic, and Galápagos penguins — similar in shape, colour, and behaviour.

questions.title: Old World
questions.stem: What makes the African penguin unique among living penguins?
choices: It is the only penguin that lives in Antarctica
It is the only penguin species that breeds on the African continent — the only penguin found in the Old World
It is the only penguin that can fly
questions.why: Wikipedia calls it the only penguin species that breeds in Africa, and the only penguin found in the Old World. Other living penguins breed in the New World or farther south.

questions.title: Salt gland
questions.stem: How does an African penguin’s supraorbital salt gland keep the body in osmotic balance?
choices: It stores seawater in the stomach until the salt evaporates
It turns salt into fresh water inside the lungs
It sits above the eyes and excretes concentrated salt, so extra salt from seawater and prey can leave the body
questions.why: African penguins have supraorbital salt glands above the eyes. The glands excrete concentrated salt, which helps maintain osmotic balance while the bird forages at sea.

questions.title: Camouflage
questions.stem: What named camouflage strategy is an African penguin’s dark back and pale belly?
choices: Classic countershading — a dark dorsal surface and pale ventral surface that hide the bird from above and below
Disruptive coloration — random blotches that hide the outline
Aposematism — bright warning colours that scare predators
questions.why: Wikipedia names the colouring as countershading, a classic camouflage strategy. The dark back blends with the water from above, and the pale belly is harder to see from below.

questions.title: Blood flow
questions.stem: What actually makes the pink facial patch above an African penguin’s eye look pinker when the bird is warmer?
choices: Sunburn that permanently dyes the skin
More blood flowing into the patch (vasodilation); less flow (vasoconstriction) when the bird is cooler
Extra salt crystals sitting on the feathers
questions.why: Blood flow controls the colour. When the bird is warmer, more blood reaches the facial patch (vasodilation), so it looks pinker. Cooler birds send less blood there (vasoconstriction).

questions.title: Decline
questions.stem: What combination of pressures has driven the sharp drop in wild African penguins?
choices: Too many icebergs crowding the beaches
Extra trees shading every nest
Prey shortage, habitat loss, and climate / ocean change acting together
questions.why: Wikipedia ties the decline to several threats at once — not enough prey, lost nesting habitat, and climate / ocean change. We do not lock a single status letter or an exact percent drop.

questions.title: Fisheries
questions.stem: How do commercial fisheries compete with African penguins near colonies?
choices: Purse-seine and other commercial boats take sardines and anchovies — the same prey the birds hunt
They harvest ice that penguins need for nests
They collect penguin eggs for fertilizer
questions.why: Commercial fishing of sardines and anchovies leaves less prey near colonies, so birds must travel farther or switch to poorer food. Purse-seine and other commercial fleets work the same waters the penguins use.

questions.title: Closures
questions.stem: Why can no-take fishing closures around African penguin colonies help breeding birds?
choices: They keep tourists from seeing the penguins
They keep more sardines and anchovies within the birds’ foraging range while chicks are being raised
They force penguins to nest on ice instead
questions.why: Closures and no-fishing zones around colonies leave more prey within a breeding bird’s reach. Wikipedia notes that restricting fishing near sites such as Robben Island improved breeding success, and later no-fishing zones were set around key breeding areas.

questions.title: Diving
questions.stem: How do African penguins usually catch their prey underwater?
choices: They sit on the surface and wait for fish to jump
They walk along the beach and pick leftover shells
They forage by pursuit diving — chasing prey underwater on relatively shallow, short dives
questions.why: Wikipedia calls the African penguin a pursuit diver. Typical dives are relatively shallow and short; we do not lock a single max depth or dive time.

questions.title: Relatives
questions.stem: What are penguins’ closest living relatives as an order?
choices: Tubenoses such as albatrosses and petrels — not ostriches or gulls
Ostriches and other flightless land birds
Gulls and other typical coastal seabirds
questions.why: Penguins (order Sphenisciformes) sit closest to the tubenoses (albatrosses, petrels, and shearwaters). They are not closest to ostriches, and not closest to gulls.

caribbean-flamingo.source_note: Facts from Wikipedia, American flamingo / Caribbean flamingo.
talk_about: Why might standing on one leg help a flamingo?
If you had a long, bendy neck, what would you look at first at the zoo?
Which other animal at the zoo lives near the water?
push_further: A flamingo’s pink colour comes from its food. What would happen if it ate different food?
Flamingos can fly, even though people often see them only wading. Why might people miss that?
Find one more bird on your zoo map that stands in water. How does it use its legs or beak?

teach: Grown-up Caribbean flamingos are bright pink.
They often stand on one leg.
They find food in shallow water.
A group of flamingos is a flock.
Baby flamingos are grey and fluffy — not bright pink at first.

questions.title: Colour
questions.stem: What colour are grown-up Caribbean flamingos?
choices: Bright pink / reddish-pink
Bright green
All black
questions.why: Adult American flamingos — also called Caribbean flamingos — have reddish-pink feathers. Wikipedia also calls them rosy flamingos because of that pink colour.

questions.title: One leg
questions.stem: How do Caribbean flamingos often stand?
choices: On their beaks
On one leg
Upside down in trees
questions.why: Flamingos often stand on one leg with the other tucked up. Wikipedia says this may help them keep warm or rest with less effort.

questions.title: Food place
questions.stem: Where do Caribbean flamingos find their food?
choices: High in rainforest trees
Only on dry desert sand
In shallow water
questions.why: They wade in shallow water — lagoons, mudflats, and shallow lakes — and stir the bottom to find small food.

questions.title: Flock
questions.stem: What do you call a group of Caribbean flamingos?
choices: A flock
A pride
A school
questions.why: Flamingos live and fly together in a flock. Wikipedia often talks about flocks of American flamingos.

questions.title: Chicks
questions.stem: What do baby Caribbean flamingos look like at first?
choices: Bright pink like the grown-ups
Grey and fluffy
Covered in shiny scales
questions.why: Chicks hatch greyish and fluffy. They are not bright pink at first — that colour comes later from their food.

questions.title: Neck
questions.stem: What is special about a Caribbean flamingo’s neck?
choices: It is short and stiff
It is made of wood
It is long and bendy
questions.why: Flamingos have a long, bendy neck. It helps them reach down into shallow water to feed.

questions.title: Nest
questions.stem: What kind of nest does a Caribbean flamingo build?
choices: A little mound of mud
A high stick nest in a tree
A hole in Antarctic ice
questions.why: Wikipedia says the American flamingo lays its egg on a mud mound. Both parents help with the nest.

questions.title: Beak
questions.stem: What is a Caribbean flamingo’s beak like?
choices: Straight like a needle
Bent in the middle (curved / angled)
Round like a spoon with no bend
questions.why: The beak is hooked downward — bent in the middle. That curved shape helps the bird filter food from the water.

questions.title: Pink from food
questions.stem: Why are grown-up Caribbean flamingos pink?
choices: They are painted pink
They are born that bright pink
The pink colour comes from the food they eat
questions.why: The pink comes from colour in their food, such as tiny shrimp and algae. They are not painted, and chicks are not born that bright pink.

questions.title: Myth buster
questions.stem: Can Caribbean flamingos fly?
choices: Yes — they are strong fliers
No — they are flightless like ostriches
Only if a zoo clips their wings first
questions.why: Flamingos are capable flyers. They fly in flocks to find food. They are not flightless.

questions.title: Carotenoids
questions.stem: What actually makes a Caribbean flamingo’s feathers pink?
choices: Carotenoid pigments in algae, shrimp, and similar food
Pink paint on the feathers
The salt in the water dyes them pink
questions.why: The pink comes from carotenoid pigments in the diet — algae, shrimp, and similar food. The body turns those pigments into feather colour. They are not painted.

questions.title: Upside-down feeding
questions.stem: How does a Caribbean flamingo hold its bill when it feeds?
choices: Straight down like a heron stabbing fish
Upside down — the head is inverted in the water
Pointed straight up at the sky
questions.why: Flamingos feed with the head upside down and the bill inverted in the water, so the bent beak can filter food.

questions.title: Lamellae
questions.stem: What do the comb-like lamellae in a Caribbean flamingo’s bill do?
choices: Sharpen the beak for cracking nuts
Help the bird whistle louder
Strain tiny food from the water
questions.why: Hairy, comb-like lamellae line the bill and strain small food from mud and water.

questions.title: Crop milk
questions.stem: How do Caribbean flamingo parents feed a newly hatched chick?
choices: Both parents can feed a nutrient-rich “crop milk” secretion
Only the mother brings whole fish
The chick hunts alone from day one
questions.why: Both the male and the female can feed the chick a crop-milk secretion from the upper digestive tract. It is rich in fat and protein.

questions.title: One egg
questions.stem: How many eggs does a Caribbean flamingo usually lay in a clutch?
choices: A dozen, like a chicken
Typically one egg
None — they adopt other birds’ eggs
questions.why: Wikipedia says the American flamingo typically lays a single chalky-white egg on a mud mound.

questions.title: One-leg why
questions.stem: Why can standing on one leg take almost no muscle effort for a flamingo?
choices: The tucked leg is glued in place
The bird is always asleep on one foot
A passive joint lock lets the pose hold with almost no muscle work
questions.why: A flamingo’s one-legged pose can be held with almost no muscle activity — a passive joint lock — so standing that way takes little effort.

questions.title: Salty home
questions.stem: Why can Caribbean flamingos thrive in very salty shallow water?
choices: Few other birds compete there, and they can handle salty or alkaline shallows
They only drink rain from leaves
They freeze the salt into ice cubes
questions.why: They live in saline lagoons, mudflats, and shallow brackish or alkaline lakes. Few competitors survive in that water, so flamingos have the shallows more to themselves.

questions.title: Vivid species
questions.stem: How does a Caribbean / American flamingo’s colour compare with other flamingo species?
choices: It is the palest flamingo
It is among the most vividly coloured — brighter pink/red than the greater flamingo
All flamingo species look identical
questions.why: Adult American flamingos are rosy-pink to reddish. Wikipedia notes they look much more vivid than the paler greater flamingo — among the brightest flamingo species.

questions.title: Courtship
questions.stem: What do Caribbean flamingo groups often do when they court?
choices: Each bird sings a solo from a tree
They wrestle in deep ocean water
They perform synchronised displays such as head-flagging and wing salutes
questions.why: Before nesting, groups perform ritual displays together — stretching necks, head-flagging, and flapping or saluting with the wings. The displays help time nesting and pair birds up.

questions.title: Pale myth
questions.stem: If a zoo flamingo looks pale, what is the usual reason?
choices: It usually needs more carotenoids in its diet — or it may be feeding a chick
It must be a different, white flamingo species
Pale feathers mean it cannot fly
questions.why: A pale flamingo is not a different species. Captive birds fade if their food does not have enough carotenoids. A parent feeding crop milk can also look paler for a while.

questions.title: Closest relatives
questions.stem: What do molecular studies place flamingos closest to among living birds?
choices: Grebes — they sit together in the clade Mirandornithes, not with herons or storks
Herons and storks — the classic long-legged waders
Pelicans and other large fish-eaters
questions.why: Molecular work groups flamingos with grebes in Mirandornithes. They were long placed with herons and storks, but that older tree does not hold.

questions.title: Feather pigment
questions.stem: What kind of pigment gives a Caribbean flamingo’s feathers their main pink colour?
choices: Melanin made in the skin, like a tattoo
A carotenoid pigment deposited in the feathers — a compound such as canthaxanthin, not a paint
Salt crystals that stain the feathers red
questions.why: The pink in the feathers is a carotenoid pigment from the diet, processed and laid down in the plumage. A compound such as canthaxanthin is an example — we do not lock one chemical name.

questions.title: Crop milk
questions.stem: Where does flamingo “crop milk” actually come from, and is it like mammalian milk?
choices: Only from the mother’s mammary glands, like cow’s milk
Only from the chick’s own stomach
A secretion from glands lining the upper digestive tract — both sexes make it; it is not mammalian milk
questions.why: Both parents secrete a fat-and-protein fluid from glands lining the upper digestive tract, not just the crop. It is not mammalian milk — no mammary glands, and it is not the same as cow’s milk.

questions.title: Tongue piston
questions.stem: How does a Caribbean flamingo’s tongue help it filter-feed?
choices: It acts like a piston, pumping water through the comb-like lamellae
It tastes the water and then the bird swallows everything
It spears fish like a heron’s bill
questions.why: The large tongue works as a piston, drawing water in and pushing it out through the lamellae so tiny food stays behind.

questions.title: Bill mechanics
questions.stem: What is unusual about a flamingo’s bill compared with most birds?
choices: The two jaws are the same size and never move
The lower mandible is the larger one, and the upper mandible can move — unusual among birds
Only the tongue moves; both jaws are fused shut
questions.why: In most birds the lower jaw is the mobile, smaller one. In flamingos the lower mandible is larger, and they can raise the upper jaw as well as drop the lower.

questions.title: Salt glands
questions.stem: How do Caribbean flamingos handle the extra salt in hypersaline lakes?
choices: They never drink
They store salt in their feathers until it blows away
Nasal salt glands help excrete concentrated salt, so extra salt can leave the body
questions.why: American flamingos have nasal salt glands that work with the kidney. The glands excrete concentrated salt through the nares, which helps them live in very salty water.

questions.title: One-leg stay
questions.stem: What biomechanical trick lets a flamingo hold a one-leg pose with almost no muscle work?
choices: Gravity can lock a passive stay at the joint, so the pose holds with little active muscle force
The tucked foot is glued to the belly
A second hidden skeleton props the body up
questions.why: Studies show the one-legged pose can be held with little or no muscle activity — a gravity-driven passive stay at the joint. The lock is mostly gravity, not extra muscle work.

questions.title: Taxonomy
questions.stem: How have scientists treated the American / Caribbean flamingo (Phoenicopterus ruber) next to the greater flamingo?
choices: They have always been two unrelated bird families
P. ruber has sometimes been lumped with, or treated next to, the greater flamingo — a split that is now widely preferred
They are the same bird as the Chilean flamingo
questions.why: The greater flamingo was once treated as a subspecies of P. ruber, or the two were lumped. Many authorities now keep them as close relatives but separate species. We do not lock one forever name.

questions.title: Chick bill
questions.stem: How does a Caribbean flamingo chick’s bill change as it grows?
choices: It starts fully hooked and then straightens
Chicks have no bill until they fledge
It starts relatively straight and bends as filter-feeding develops
questions.why: Hatchlings begin with a relatively straight bill. The familiar downward bend develops as the young bird grows into filter-feeding.

questions.title: Status
questions.stem: How does the wild status of the American / Caribbean flamingo compare with many other zoo-card animals?
choices: It is relatively secure compared with many zoo-card species — often treated as a lower-risk listing
It is always the most threatened bird on Earth
It went extinct in the 1800s
questions.why: Wild American / Caribbean flamingos are often treated as relatively secure next to several more threatened zoo-card animals. We do not lock a single status letter.

talk_about: Why might a hard shell help a tortoise?
If you could live over 100 years, what would you want to see at the zoo?
Which other animal at the zoo has a shell or a hard covering?
push_further: A tortoise cannot leave its shell. How is that different from taking off a coat?
Galápagos tortoises move slowly. What might they notice that a fast animal would miss?
Find one more animal on your zoo map that eats plants. How does it reach its food?

teach: They live on islands near Ecuador in the Pacific (the Galápagos).
They are among the largest tortoises in the world.
They can live over 100 years.
They eat plants: grass, leaves, and cactus.
The hard covering on their back is a shell.

questions.title: Home
questions.stem: Where do wild Galápagos tortoises live?
choices: On islands near Ecuador in the Pacific (the Galápagos)
On the ice in Antarctica
Only in African deserts
questions.why: They live on the Galápagos Islands in the Pacific Ocean, near Ecuador. That island home is why they are called Galápagos tortoises.

questions.title: Size
questions.stem: How big is a Galápagos tortoise?
choices: Among the smallest turtles
Among the largest tortoises in the world
About the size of a mouse
questions.why: Galápagos tortoises are giant tortoises — among the largest in the world. Wikipedia calls them the largest living tortoise.

questions.title: Age
questions.stem: How long can a Galápagos tortoise live?
choices: Only a few weeks
Just one summer
Over 100 years
questions.why: Wild Galápagos tortoises can live over 100 years. They are among the longest-lived animals.

questions.title: Food
questions.stem: What do Galápagos tortoises eat?
choices: Plants such as grass, leaves, and cactus
Mostly meat
Only fish
questions.why: They are plant-eaters. Wikipedia lists grasses, leaves, and cactus among the plants they nibble.

questions.title: Shell
questions.stem: What is the hard covering on a Galápagos tortoise’s back?
choices: A backpack
A shell
A hat
questions.why: The hard covering on the back is a shell. It protects the tortoise’s body.

questions.title: Speed
questions.stem: How does a Galápagos tortoise usually move?
choices: It sprints like a cheetah
It flies
It moves slowly
questions.why: Galápagos tortoises walk slowly. They are famous for being slow and steady.

questions.title: Eggs
questions.stem: How do baby Galápagos tortoises start life?
choices: They hatch from eggs buried in the ground
They are born in the water like fish
They grow on trees
questions.why: Mothers bury eggs in a nest in the ground. Later, the babies hatch and dig out.

questions.title: Hide
questions.stem: What can a Galápagos tortoise do when it is frightened?
choices: Climb a tall tree
Pull its head and legs inside its shell
Shoot water from its shell
questions.why: When frightened, it can pull its head, neck, and legs inside the shell for safety.

questions.title: Neck
questions.stem: What is special about a Galápagos tortoise’s neck?
choices: It is too short to reach food
It is made of metal
It is long and can stretch upward to reach food
questions.why: Many Galápagos tortoises have a long neck that can stretch up to reach leaves and cactus.

questions.title: Myth buster
questions.stem: Can a Galápagos tortoise leave its shell?
choices: No — the shell is part of its skeleton
Yes — the shell is a coat it takes off
Only at night
questions.why: The shell is part of the tortoise’s skeleton, not a coat. It cannot leave its shell.

questions.title: Shell shapes
questions.stem: What are the two main Galápagos tortoise shell shapes?
choices: Domed and saddleback
Spiky and flat
Square and triangular
questions.why: Wikipedia describes two main shell forms: a rounded domed shell and a saddleback shell with a raised front edge.

questions.title: Saddleback why
questions.stem: Why does a saddleback Galápagos tortoise have a raised front notch on its shell?
choices: It helps the tortoise swim faster
The raised front notch helps it stretch up to reach high plants on drier islands
It is painted on as a decoration
questions.why: Saddleback shells arch upward at the front so the tortoise can lift its neck and browse taller plants on dry islands, where less food grows on the ground.

questions.title: Long fasting
questions.stem: How long can a Galápagos tortoise go without food or water?
choices: Only a few hours
It must eat every single day
A long time — many months, or about a year
questions.why: They can go many months without drinking, and Wikipedia says they can endure about a year without food and water. We do not lock a longer extreme.

questions.title: Water store
questions.stem: Where can a Galápagos tortoise store water?
choices: In the bladder and other body tissues
Only in a backpack on the shell
They never store water at all
questions.why: After a big drink they can store water in the bladder and in body tissues. That store helps them through dry spells.

questions.title: Darwin
questions.stem: Why are Galápagos tortoises famous in the story of evolution?
choices: They taught Darwin how to swim
Island-to-island differences helped inspire Darwin’s thinking on evolution
Darwin invented the tortoise
questions.why: Darwin saw that tortoises looked different from island to island. Those differences helped him think about how living things can change over time.

questions.title: Sailor history
questions.stem: Why did Galápagos tortoise numbers crash in the 1800s?
choices: A sudden ice age froze the islands
The tortoises all flew away
Sailors took huge numbers as long-lasting shipboard food
questions.why: In the 1800s, whalers and other sailors collected live tortoises because they lasted a long time on board without food or water. That hunting crashed wild numbers.

questions.title: Introduced pests
questions.stem: How do introduced goats, rats, and pigs harm Galápagos tortoises?
choices: Goats eat the plants; rats and pigs destroy eggs and hatchlings
They only scare the tortoises with noise
They teach the tortoises to fly
questions.why: Introduced goats compete for food and strip plants. Rats and pigs eat eggs and young tortoises, so few hatchlings survive.

questions.title: Lonesome George
questions.stem: Who was Lonesome George?
choices: The first tortoise Darwin rode
The last known Pinta Island tortoise; he died in 2012
A famous sea turtle from Florida
questions.why: Lonesome George was the last known tortoise from Pinta Island. He lived at the breeding centre and died in 2012.

questions.title: Breeding success
questions.stem: How has captive breeding helped Galápagos tortoises?
choices: Captive breeding has never worked
Zoos painted extra shells to look like more tortoises
It has helped rebuild some island groups — famous breeding males such as Diego fathered many young
questions.why: Breeding centres have raised and released many young. Famous males such as Diego helped a depleted island population recover. We do not lock one exact offspring count.

questions.title: Tortoise vs turtle
questions.stem: How is a tortoise different from a sea turtle?
choices: Tortoises live on land and have column-like feet, not flippers like sea turtles
Tortoises have flippers and live only in the ocean
Tortoises and sea turtles are the same animal
questions.why: A tortoise is a land-living turtle. Galápagos tortoises walk on sturdy, column-like legs. Sea turtles have flippers for swimming.

questions.title: Genus
questions.stem: Which genus do Galápagos tortoises belong in today?
choices: Chelonoidis — they sit with the South American clade, not Geochelone or Testudo
Geochelone — the old catch-all for typical land tortoises
Testudo — the Mediterranean tortoise genus
questions.why: Wikipedia places Galápagos tortoises in Chelonoidis with other South American tortoises. They were long filed in Geochelone or Testudo; those older genus names do not hold.

questions.title: Species complex
questions.stem: How do scientists treat the named Galápagos tortoise island forms?
choices: As one unnamed population with no island differences
As a species complex — roughly a dozen-plus named taxa or island forms, and whether they are species or subspecies is still debated
As exactly two species that never mix or vary
questions.why: Named island forms make a species complex. Counts and ranks shift as studies arrive, so we say roughly a dozen-plus taxa rather than locking one number.

questions.title: Adaptive radiation
questions.stem: Why are Galápagos tortoise shell differences a textbook evolutionary case?
choices: Every island tortoise has the same shell because they never evolve
Shells were painted different colours by tourists
Divergent shell shapes across islands are a textbook adaptive radiation — forms evolved to match different island habitats
questions.why: Island-to-island shell divergence is a classic adaptive radiation: related lineages evolved different forms in different habitats. We do not treat one shape name as the whole story.

questions.title: Low metabolism
questions.stem: What physiological traits let a Galápagos tortoise tolerate a long fast?
choices: Ectothermy plus a very low metabolic rate, so they can last a long time without food
A warm-blooded, high-energy metabolism like a hummingbird
They photosynthesize through the shell
questions.why: They are ectotherms with a very slow metabolism. That low energy use, not a locked day-count, is why they can go a long time without eating.

questions.title: Carapace anatomy
questions.stem: What is a Galápagos tortoise’s carapace largely built from?
choices: A hollow plastic box glued onto the back
Fused ribs and vertebrae, overlain by keratin scutes
Loose scales that fall off each winter
questions.why: The bony carapace is largely fused ribs and vertebrae. Keratin scutes overlie that bone. Wikipedia notes the plates are fused with the ribs in a rigid structure integral to the body.

questions.title: Pinta extinction
questions.stem: What is the status of the Pinta Island tortoise, C. abingdonii?
choices: It is the most common wild tortoise on every island
It was never a real island form
C. abingdonii is treated as functionally extinct after Lonesome George died in 2012
questions.why: The Pinta form C. abingdonii is treated as functionally extinct. Lonesome George, the last known individual, died in 2012. Hybrids have been discussed, but the pure Pinta lineage is gone.

questions.title: Fernandina rediscovery
questions.stem: What happened to the Fernandina Island tortoise, long presumed extinct?
choices: A living female was found in recent years after the form was long presumed extinct
It was proven never to have lived on Fernandina
It was moved to Antarctica in the 1800s
questions.why: The Fernandina tortoise was long presumed extinct after a single old specimen. A living female turned up in recent years (late 2010s) and was taken to a breeding centre. We do not lock one calendar year.

questions.title: Megaherbivores
questions.stem: What ecological role do Galápagos tortoises play on their islands?
choices: They only sit still and never change the habitat
They act as megaherbivores and ecosystem engineers — dispersing seeds and shaping vegetation
They only eat fish and leave plants untouched
questions.why: Wikipedia calls them keystone ecosystem engineers. They disperse seeds and trample or thin vegetation, which changes what can grow.

questions.title: Genome
questions.stem: What did genome studies of Lonesome George highlight?
choices: That giant tortoises have no DNA at all
A single gene that makes the shell detach
Variants linked to DNA-repair, immune, and tumour-suppression pathways — we do not lock exact gene names
questions.why: Sequencing Lonesome George highlighted variants tied to DNA repair, immune function, and tumour-suppression pathways. Exact gene names stay unlocked because lists keep shifting.

questions.title: Hatchling sex
questions.stem: How is the sex of a Galápagos tortoise hatchling determined?
choices: By incubation temperature — temperature-dependent sex determination, not sex chromosomes
By X and Y sex chromosomes, as in mammals
By the colour of the mother’s shell
questions.why: Hatchling sex is temperature-dependent. Cooler nests tend to yield more males and warmer nests more females. It is not an XX/XY chromosome system.

talk_about: Why might unique stripes help a keeper or a scientist tell zebras apart?
If stripes deter flies, what other “weird” animal traits might have unexpected jobs?
How is a zebra family like a lion pride — and how is it different?
push_further: Compare zebra digestion (hindgut) with a giraffe or cow (ruminant) at the zoo.
Find another striped animal on your map — same reason for stripes, or different?
Quagga Project tries to breed back a quagga-like look — what does “extinct” mean if genes live on in relatives?

teach: They have bold black-and-white stripes — each zebra’s pattern is unique.
They mostly eat grass (plants, not meat).
They live on African grassland / savanna.
They live in family groups that can join bigger herds.
A baby zebra is a foal.

questions.title: Stripes
questions.stem: What is special about a plains zebra’s coat?
choices: Bold black-and-white stripes — and each zebra’s pattern is unique
All zebras share one identical stripe pattern
They are solid brown with no stripes
questions.why: Wikipedia says plains zebras are boldly striped in black and white, and no two individuals look exactly alike.

questions.title: Food
questions.stem: What do plains zebras mostly eat?
choices: Meat
Grass (plants, not meat)
Only fish
questions.why: Plains zebras primarily feed on grass. They are plant-eaters, not meat-eaters.

questions.title: Home
questions.stem: Where do wild plains zebras live?
choices: The ice in Antarctica
Only in deep rainforest
African grassland / savanna
questions.why: Wikipedia says their habitat is generally treeless grasslands and savanna woodlands in Africa.

questions.title: Family
questions.stem: How do plains zebras live together?
choices: In family groups (a stallion with mares and young) that can join bigger herds
Always completely alone
Only in pairs of two
questions.why: They live in family groups — a stallion, several mares, and their young. Those groups can come together to form bigger herds.

questions.title: Baby
questions.stem: What do you call a baby plains zebra?
choices: A cub
A foal
A chick
questions.why: A baby zebra is a foal — the same word used for a baby horse.

questions.title: Speed
questions.stem: How do plains zebras escape danger?
choices: They fly away
They hide underground
They can run fast
questions.why: An adult zebra can run fast to get away from lions and other hunters. We do not lock one exact speed.

questions.title: Horse kin
questions.stem: What animal is a plains zebra a wild relative of?
choices: The horse (same horse family)
The house cat
The penguin
questions.why: Zebras belong to the horse family. They are wild relatives of the horse, not a farm pet.

questions.title: Mane
questions.stem: What is a plains zebra’s mane like?
choices: Long and floppy like a farm horse’s mane
Short and upright along the neck
Missing — zebras have no mane
questions.why: Like other wild horses, a plains zebra has a short, upright mane along the neck.

questions.title: Voice
questions.stem: What contact call is a plains zebra known for?
choices: A roar like a lion
A moo like a cow
A barking / “kwaha” call
questions.why: Wikipedia describes a high-pitched contact call, often called barking — heard as “kwaha” or similar.

questions.title: Myth buster
questions.stem: Are plains zebras just striped farm horses you can ride?
choices: No — they are wild animals, not domesticated like horses
Yes — they are tame like farm horses
Only if you paint extra stripes on
questions.why: Zebras are wild, not domesticated like horses. They are horse relatives, but they are not farm horses you can ride the same way.

questions.title: Fly-stripe idea
questions.stem: What is a leading idea today for why plains zebras have stripes?
choices: Stripes help deter biting flies
The stripes are only for looking pretty to people
Scientists have proved stripes are only for hiding in tall grass
questions.why: A leading idea today is that the stripe pattern helps deter biting flies. Camouflage and heat-only explanations are still discussed, so this is a hypothesis — not a finished proof.

questions.title: Harem
questions.stem: What is a plains zebra harem?
choices: A pair of two zebras that never meet others
One stallion, several mares, and their young
Only bachelor males living together
questions.why: Wikipedia says plains zebras form harems with a single stallion, several mares, and their recent offspring.

questions.title: Bachelor groups
questions.stem: What do young male plains zebras often do before starting a harem?
choices: They live completely alone from birth
They immediately take over the family they were born into
They often form bachelor groups of other young males
questions.why: Young males often join bachelor groups until they are ready to start a harem of their own.

questions.title: Pioneer grazer
questions.stem: Why are plains zebras often called pioneer grazers?
choices: They are often first to graze tall, tough grass, and other grazers follow the shorter growth
They wait until other animals eat first
They only eat fruit from trees
questions.why: Zebras are pioneer grazers — often first into tall, tough grass. More specialised grazers such as wildebeest and gazelles follow the shorter growth.

questions.title: Hindgut
questions.stem: How does a plains zebra digest grass compared with a cow-like ruminant?
choices: It chews a cud like a cow
It is a hindgut fermenter — food moves through faster, so it is less picky
It does not digest plants at all
questions.why: Zebras are hindgut fermenters. Food passes through faster than in ruminants, so they are less selective and spend a lot of time eating.

questions.title: Water need
questions.stem: How tied are plains zebras to drinking water?
choices: They can go months without a drink
They only drink seawater
They are water-dependent and seldom wander far from drinking water
questions.why: Plains zebras are water-dependent. They seldom wander far from a drinking source.

questions.title: Alarm
questions.stem: What do plains zebras often do when they spot a predator?
choices: They bark or snort, and the group stays alert
They stay silent and freeze for hours
They roar like lions
questions.why: They keep watch for predators. They bark or snort when they see one, and the group stays alert.

questions.title: Foal coat
questions.stem: What colour are a newborn plains zebra’s stripes at first?
choices: Bright neon green
Brownish — they darken with age
Already jet-black on day one, never changing
questions.why: A foal’s natal coat is brown and white. The brown darkens with age.

questions.title: Shadow stripes
questions.stem: What extra marking do some southern plains zebras show between the black and white?
choices: Gold spots like a giraffe
Blue rings on every hoof
Brown “shadow” stripes — commoner in some southern populations
questions.why: Some southern plains zebras show brown “shadow” stripes between the black and white. They are absent or faint in many northern zebras, so this is “some populations,” not every zebra.

questions.title: Threats
questions.stem: What puts wild plains zebras under pressure today?
choices: Hunting and habitat loss / farming encroachment
Too many zoos
They have no wild threats
questions.why: Wikipedia says they are threatened by hunting for meat and hide, plus livestock competition and farming that takes over grassland. We do not lock a status letter.

questions.title: Species name
questions.stem: What scientific name do scientists use for the plains zebra today?
choices: Equus quagga — older books often used Equus burchellii
Equus caballus — the same name as the farm horse
Panthera leo
questions.why: Wikipedia lists the plains zebra as Equus quagga. It was once classified as Equus burchellii; after the quagga was shown to belong with this species, the older name quagga took priority.

questions.title: Three living zebras
questions.stem: The plains zebra is one of how many living zebra species?
choices: The only zebra species on Earth
One of three living species — with Grévy’s zebra and the mountain zebra
One of twenty living horse species, all called zebras
questions.why: Wikipedia treats three living zebra species: plains, Grévy’s, and mountain. The plains zebra is the most common and widespread of the three.

questions.title: Quagga
questions.stem: What do DNA studies say about the extinct quagga and today’s plains zebra?
choices: The quagga was an unrelated striped cow
Scientists proved the quagga was a forever-separate species with no living relatives
DNA supports a close relationship — a southern plains-zebra form in the same species complex
questions.why: Genetic work found the quagga belongs with plains zebras, not a distant species. Wikipedia notes DNA supports that close relationship. Later work also talks about a north–south continuum, so we do not lock “subspecies forever.”

questions.title: Stripe cline
questions.stem: How does plains-zebra striping tend to change from north to south?
choices: Striping tends to lessen toward the south, and brown “shadow” stripes are more common in southern populations
Every plains zebra has the same complete stripe set
Southern zebras lose all stripes and turn solid white
questions.why: Northern plains zebras tend to have narrower, more complete stripes. Toward the south, striping often thins on the belly, legs, and hindquarters, and brown “shadow” stripes show up more often. Researchers also describe this as a cline more than a forever subspecies list.

questions.title: Fly deterrence
questions.stem: What does experimental and comparative research currently favor as a leading job of zebra stripes?
choices: Scientists have proved stripes exist only to hide from lions
Work on biting flies favors fly deterrence as a leading idea — still debated against camouflage and heat
Stripes have no possible function at all
questions.why: Experimental and comparative studies cited on Wikipedia point to biting-fly deterrence as a leading explanation. Camouflage and heat-control ideas are still discussed, so the question is not closed.

questions.title: Flehmen
questions.stem: How does a stallion check whether a mare is ready to mate?
choices: He counts her stripes
He waits for her to roar
He uses flehmen — curling the upper lip to smell urine via the vomeronasal organ
questions.why: Wikipedia says males show the flehmen response: the upper lip curls back so they can test urine with the vomeronasal organ and check if a mare is receptive.

questions.title: Harem takeover
questions.stem: What often happens to a plains zebra harem when a new stallion takes over?
choices: The new stallion may take over gradually, and adult mare membership often stays intact
All the mares immediately leave and live alone
