The whole family always splits into single animals
questions.why: Wikipedia says a new stallion may push an unhealthy rival out gradually, without a big fight. The adult mares of a harem usually stay together even when the stallion changes.

questions.title: Foal protection
questions.stem: What does a mother plains zebra do with her newborn at first?
choices: She hands the foal to the stallion on day one
She keeps other zebras — even the stallion — away until the foal and group can bond
She hides the foal underground for a month
questions.why: Early on, a mother keeps any other zebra away from her foal, including the stallion, other mares, and even her previous young. Later they all bond.

questions.title: Migration memory
questions.stem: What do studies suggest migratory plains-zebra herds use to find good grazing?
choices: Only what they can see that same morning
A written map they pass from parent to foal
Memory of places where foraging was good — not only day-to-day perception
questions.why: Wikipedia cites research that migrating zebras appear to rely on some memory of where foraging was best, and may even anticipate conditions later on. That is a research finding, not a claim that they never look around.

questions.title: Status snapshot
questions.stem: What do scientists emphasize about wild plains-zebra numbers today?
choices: Hunting and habitat change put many populations under pressure — a snapshot listing has been Near Threatened
They have no human-made pressures at all
They were declared extinct worldwide
questions.why: Wikipedia emphasizes hunting for meat and hide, plus farming and livestock competition. IUCN has listed the plains zebra Near Threatened — we treat that letter as a snapshot, not a forever grade.

talk_about: Hippos often walk or bounce on the river bottom. How is that different from a fish that swims?
Why might a bull hippo hold a stretch of water, but show little territoriality on land?
A wheeze-honk can travel a long way. What might a hippo be saying to the rest of the pod?
push_further: The reddish skin goo is sunscreen and can help fight microbes. What other “weird” animal traits might have unexpected jobs?
A hippo’s closest living relatives are whales and dolphins. What still surprises you about that?
Hippos rest in pods in the water, then graze alone on land. Why might bachelor bulls stay near the edge?

teach: Their name comes from Greek for “horse of the river.”
They stay cool in water or mud by day, then graze on land at dusk.
In the wild they eat almost all grass — not fish.
Eyes, ears, and nostrils sit high so they can rest with most of the body under water.
The reddish “blood sweat” is a sunscreen goo — not blood and not sweat.

questions.title: River horse
questions.stem: What does the name hippopotamus mean?
choices: Horse of the river
Desert camel
Flying fish
questions.why: Wikipedia says the name comes from Ancient Greek for “horse of the river.”

questions.title: Day and night
questions.stem: What do Nile hippos usually do by day and at dusk?
choices: Hunt fish all day and sleep on rocks at night
Stay cool in water or mud by day, then graze on land at dusk
Fly south when the sun is out
questions.why: Hippos remain cool by staying in water or mud during the day, then come out at dusk to graze.

questions.title: Grass, not fish
questions.stem: What do wild Nile hippos mostly eat?
choices: Fish they catch with their tusks
Only zoo popcorn
Almost all grass
questions.why: A wild hippo’s diet is almost entirely grass, with only a little aquatic plant matter — not fish.

questions.title: Periscope face
questions.stem: Why are a Nile hippo’s eyes, ears, and nostrils high on its head?
choices: So it can rest in water with most of its body hidden
So it can hang from trees
So it can smell clouds
questions.why: Those parts sit high on the skull so they can stay above the water while the rest of the body is submerged.

questions.title: “Blood sweat”
questions.stem: What is the reddish liquid people call a hippo’s “blood sweat”?
choices: Blood the hippo sweats when it is hot
A sunscreen goo — not blood and not sweat
River mud that never washes off
questions.why: People nickname it “blood sweat,” but it is neither blood nor sweat. It is a red-colored sunscreen secretion.

questions.title: Surprise cousins
questions.stem: Who are a hippo’s closest living relatives?
choices: Farm pigs, because they look alike
Crocodiles that share the same river
Whales and dolphins — a surprise for many people
questions.why: Hippos can look a bit like pigs, but their closest living relatives are whales and dolphins.

questions.title: Huge yawn
questions.stem: What does a hippo’s huge “yawn” usually mean?
choices: The wide-open mouth is a threat — the tusks are for fighting, not chewing grass
It is chewing grass with its long tusks
It is catching flying birds
questions.why: The big “yawn” is a threat display. Tusks are mainly for fighting. Hippos pull grass with their lips, not those long teeth.

questions.title: Stay back
questions.stem: Why do people treat wild hippos with extra care?
choices: They are tiny and easy to pick up
They can be dangerous when surprised or when a mother is guarding a calf
They only live in picture books
questions.why: Hippos are strong and can be aggressive if they are surprised or protecting young. Give them space.

questions.title: Water babies
questions.stem: Where do Nile hippos often have babies, and how can calves drink milk?
choices: Only in desert dunes; calves never drink
In nests at the tops of trees
Mating and birth often happen in water; calves can nurse underwater, and moms are protective
questions.why: Mating and birth often occur in water. Calves can nurse underwater. Mothers stay very protective of their young.

questions.title: Myth buster
questions.stem: Can a Nile hippo stay dry on land all day like a horse?
choices: No — its mostly hairless thick skin can crack if it stays dry too long
Yes — its skin never needs water
Yes — it has a heavy fur coat that holds water
questions.why: The name means “horse of the river,” but a hippo is not a horse that can stay dry all day. Hippos have little hair. Their thick skin still needs water or mud, or it can crack even with the sunscreen goo.

questions.title: Walk the bottom
questions.stem: How do Nile hippos usually move when they are underwater?
choices: They walk or bounce along the bottom — true swimming is debated
They swim like fish with a long tail
They fly just under the surface
questions.why: Wikipedia says they move in the water by walking or bouncing off the bottom. Whether they truly swim is still debated.

questions.title: Water territory
questions.stem: Where does a bull Nile hippo usually hold territory?
choices: A big patch of grassland he patrols all night
A stretch of water — they show little territoriality on land while grazing
Only a nest in a tree
questions.why: Territorial bulls preside over a stretch of water. Hippos typically do not display territorial behaviour on land while they graze.

questions.title: Pods
questions.stem: How do Nile hippos usually group up in water versus on land?
choices: They live alone in the water and graze in huge herds at night
They always stay in one tight family on land and in water
They rest in pods in the water, then typically graze alone at night
questions.why: Hippos rest near each other in the water, but grazing is a solitary activity and they typically come out at night to eat.

questions.title: Wheeze-honk
questions.stem: What is a Nile hippo’s best-known long-carrying contact call?
choices: A wheeze-honk that can travel a long way through the air
A lion-like roar that only works underwater
A silent blink that only calves can see
questions.why: The most common hippo vocalisation is the wheeze-honk, which can travel over long distances in air.

questions.title: Among the giants
questions.stem: Where does a Nile hippo sit among the largest land mammals?
choices: It is smaller than a house cat
After elephants and rhinos, it is among the next-largest land mammals
It is the only giant mammal that ever lived
questions.why: After elephants and rhinoceroses, the hippopotamus is among the next-largest land mammals. Weights vary, so we keep the ranking soft.

questions.title: Skin goo jobs
questions.stem: Besides showing it is not blood, what jobs can a hippo’s reddish skin goo do?
choices: It is only for painting zoo walls
It turns the hippo into a fish
It works as a sunscreen and can help fight microbes
questions.why: The red secretion is a natural sunscreen and can inhibit disease-causing bacteria. We skip the chemical names.

questions.title: Must breathe
questions.stem: What must a Nile hippo still do even when it rests under water?
choices: Come up to breathe regularly — even during submerged rest
Hold its breath for days like a whale
Grow gills after sunset
questions.why: Hippos must surface regularly to breathe. They can rest while submerged and still come up for air, seemingly without waking.

questions.title: Home waters
questions.stem: Where do wild Nile hippos live?
choices: Only on Arctic ice
Rivers, lakes, and mangrove swamps in sub-Saharan Africa
Only in city fountains
questions.why: Hippos inhabit rivers, lakes, and mangrove swamps. They are native to sub-Saharan Africa.

questions.title: Threats
questions.stem: What puts wild Nile hippos under pressure today?
choices: Too many birthday cakes
They have no wild threats
Habitat loss, plus hunting for meat and teeth
questions.why: They are threatened by habitat loss and hunting for meat and teeth. We do not lock a status letter.

questions.title: Calf ride
questions.stem: How can a Nile hippo calf travel with its mother in deep water?
choices: It rides on her back
It flies above her
It hitches a ride on a crocodile
questions.why: Young are carried on their mothers’ backs in deep water.

questions.title: Skin pigments
questions.stem: What are the red and orange chemicals in a hippo’s skin goo?
choices: Hipposudoric acids — red and orange pigments that can block UV and fight microbes
Blood cells that leak when the hippo is hot
River dye the hippo drinks for colour
questions.why: Wikipedia names two highly acidic pigments: red hipposudoric acid and orange norhipposudoric acid. They absorb ultraviolet light and can inhibit disease-causing bacteria. Food does not appear to be their source.

questions.title: Whale clade
questions.stem: What do scientists say hippos share with living whales and dolphins?
choices: Nothing — hippos are just river pigs with no whale relatives
A clade: their closest living relatives are cetaceans, from a shared ancestor long ago
Hippos evolved from modern killer whales last century
questions.why: Blood proteins, DNA, and the fossil record point to cetaceans — whales, dolphins, and porpoises — as the closest living relatives. Wikipedia cites a split tens of millions of years ago; we keep that dating soft because the exact million-year figures are debated. Extinct anthracotheres sit on the hippo side of that split.

questions.title: Named subspecies
questions.stem: How useful are the named Nile hippo subspecies to people who study them in the field?
choices: Every field guide locks five subspecies and uses them every day
Scientists proved there is only one hippo on Earth and no local forms
Several subspecies have been described, but they are rarely used in the field — some mitochondrial DNA shows modest support
questions.why: Wikipedia lists several described subspecies based on skulls and range. Field biologists rarely used or validated them. A mitochondrial DNA study found low but significant differences among some named forms. That is support, not a forever subspecies list — some names were never tested.

questions.title: Colombia herd
questions.stem: Where did a wild hippo population start from animals that escaped a private collection?
choices: In Colombia — a feral herd descended from hippos kept on Pablo Escobar’s estate
Only on Antarctic ice
In every city fountain worldwide
questions.why: Wikipedia says a population in Colombia descended from captives that escaped after Escobar’s death. The herd grew and is treated as an invasive problem far from African home waters.

questions.title: Pseudoruminant gut
questions.stem: How does a Nile hippo’s stomach compare with a cow that chews cud?
choices: It has no stomach at all
It is a pseudoruminant: a three-chambered stomach, but it does not chew cud
It chews cud like a cow and has four full stomach rooms
questions.why: Wikipedia calls the hippo a pseudoruminant. It has a complex three-chambered stomach but does not “chew cud.” Grass is pulled with the lips and ground on the molars.

questions.title: Status snapshot
questions.stem: How do scientists usually describe the wild status of the common / Nile hippo today?
choices: They have no human-made pressures at all
They were declared extinct worldwide
Habitat loss and poaching put them under pressure — a snapshot listing has been Vulnerable
questions.why: Wikipedia emphasizes habitat loss and poaching for meat and ivory-like canine teeth. IUCN has listed the species Vulnerable — we treat that letter as a snapshot, not a forever grade.

questions.title: Air and water cry
questions.stem: What is unusual about how a Nile hippo can send a call?
choices: They can send a cry through air and water at once, and underwater clicks have been reported
They can only tap Morse code on rocks
They have no voices at all
questions.why: Wikipedia says a hippo can hold its head partly above water and send a cry that travels through both water and air. Listeners answer above and below. Clicks underwater have been recorded and may have echolocative properties.

questions.title: Fighting teeth
questions.stem: What is special about a Nile hippo’s big canines and incisors?
choices: They are baby teeth that fall out in a week
They keep growing and are used mainly for fighting, not for chewing grass
They are hollow straws for drinking only
questions.why: On the lower jaw, incisors and canines grow continuously. They are used mainly for combat, not feeding. Hippos pull grass with flattened lips, then grind it on the molars.

questions.title: Heavy bones
questions.stem: How does a Nile hippo’s skeleton help it move in water?
choices: Hollow bird bones make it float like a duck
A springy tail propels it like a shark
Dense, graviportal bones help it sink and walk the bottom
questions.why: Wikipedia says the skeleton is graviportal — built to carry huge weight — and dense bones plus a low centre of gravity let hippos sink and move along the bottom.

questions.title: Two living hippos
questions.stem: How many living hippo species do scientists recognise today?
choices: Two: the common / Nile hippo (Hippopotamus amphibius) and the pygmy hippo
Dozens of living hippo species on every continent
Only fossil hippos — none are alive
questions.why: Wikipedia says the common hippopotamus and the pygmy hippopotamus (Choeropsis liberiensis or Hexaprotodon liberiensis) are the only living members of Hippopotamidae.

talk_about: Why might hiding in forest cover help a tiger more than living on open grassland?
If you saw a tiger swim, what would that tell you about the “afraid of water” story?
Which other animal at the zoo has stripes — same job, or different?
push_further: A threat letter on a list can change. Why treat it as a snapshot, not a forever grade?
A Sumatran tiger is smaller than many mainland tigers. What else looks different at the zoo?
Find one more cat on your zoo map. Does it live alone or in a group?

teach: Wild Sumatran tigers live only on the island of Sumatra.
They are among the smallest living tigers.
Their stripes are extra busy, with little spots between the stripes.
They hunt in forest, not open grassland like lions.
They eat meat — deer, wild pigs, and other forest prey.

questions.title: Sumatra only
questions.stem: Where do wild Sumatran tigers live?
choices: Only on the island of Sumatra
All across Asia
Only in African forests
questions.why: Wikipedia says the Sumatran tiger lives on the Indonesian island of Sumatra — not all of Asia.

questions.title: Smallest living tiger
questions.stem: How does a Sumatran tiger’s size compare with other living tigers?
choices: It is the biggest cat on Earth
It is among the smallest living tigers
It is as big as an African elephant
questions.why: Wikipedia calls the Sumatran tiger one of the smallest tigers. We do not lock one weight.

questions.title: Busy stripes
questions.stem: What is special about a Sumatran tiger’s stripes?
choices: They are fewer than on any other tiger
They are painted on at the zoo
They are denser, with little spots between the stripes
questions.why: Wikipedia says Sumatran tigers have more stripes than other tigers, and lines of small dark spots sit between the regular stripes.

questions.title: Forest cat
questions.stem: What kind of place do Sumatran tigers prefer?
choices: Forest with cover, not open grassland
Open grassland like a lion’s savannah
Sandy desert with no trees
questions.why: Wikipedia says they strongly prefer forest with dense cover. They are not open-grassland cats like lions.

questions.title: Meat hunter
questions.stem: What do wild Sumatran tigers hunt?
choices: Grass and leaves
Deer, wild pigs, and other forest prey
Only zoo snacks
questions.why: Wikipedia lists forest prey such as sambar deer, muntjac, and wild pigs (banded pigs).

questions.title: Mostly alone
questions.stem: How do Sumatran tigers usually live?
choices: In a big pride like lions
In huge flocks that never split up
Mostly alone, not in a lion-style pride
questions.why: Wikipedia’s Tiger page says a tiger lives a mostly solitary life — mostly alone, not pride life like lions.

questions.title: Cub
questions.stem: What do you call a baby Sumatran tiger?
choices: A cub
A calf
A chick
questions.why: A baby tiger is a cub — the same word used for a baby lion.

questions.title: Male ruff
questions.stem: What extra fur can a male Sumatran tiger show?
choices: A peacock tail
A cheek and neck ruff
A long horse mane down the back
questions.why: Wikipedia says males have a prominent ruff, and it is especially marked in the Sumatran tiger.

questions.title: Last Sunda tiger
questions.stem: Why is the Sumatran tiger called the last Sunda island tiger?
choices: Tigers never lived on any other island
Every island in Asia still has wild tigers
Bali and Javan tigers are gone, so Sumatra is the last of those islands
questions.why: Wikipedia says it is the only surviving tiger population in the Sunda Islands after the Bali and Javan tigers went extinct.

questions.title: Myth buster — water
questions.stem: Are Sumatran tigers scared of water, like a cartoon house cat?
choices: No — tigers are strong swimmers
Yes — they never get wet
They can only walk on frozen ice
questions.why: Wikipedia’s Tiger page says the tiger is a powerful swimmer and readily uses water, especially on hot days — not a water-scared cartoon cat.

questions.title: Understory cover
questions.stem: Why do Sumatran tigers need thick cover on the forest floor?
choices: Thick understory cover hides them; without it they are more exposed
They only hunt in wide-open fields
They nest in the tops of the tallest trees
questions.why: Wikipedia says they prefer forest with dense understory cover. Ground-level vegetation is a basic need; without it they are even more exposed to people.

questions.title: Natural forest first
questions.stem: Which kind of land do Sumatran tigers use most?
choices: They prefer busy city parks
They strongly prefer uncultivated forest and make little use of plantations
They live mainly in open grassland
questions.why: Wikipedia says Sumatran tigers strongly prefer uncultivated forests and make little use of plantations even when those plantings are nearby.

questions.title: Forest prey
questions.stem: What kinds of animals do Sumatran tigers usually hunt in the forest?
choices: Only insects and nectar
Seaweed and coral
Deer, wild pigs, and other mid-sized forest mammals
questions.why: Wikipedia lists forest prey such as sambar deer, muntjac, mouse-deer, and wild pigs, plus other mid-sized mammals. We keep the list soft.

questions.title: Fragmented pockets
questions.stem: How is Sumatran tiger habitat spread across the island?
choices: In small, scattered habitat patches across Sumatra
One unbroken forest covering every island in Asia
Only on a single city block
questions.why: Wikipedia says they persist in small, fragmented populations across Sumatra, in habitat patches spread around the island.

questions.title: Threats
questions.stem: What puts wild Sumatran tigers under pressure today?
choices: Too many birthday cakes
Habitat loss, fewer prey animals, and hunting or snares
They have no wild threats
questions.why: Wikipedia names habitat loss, prey-base depletion, and hunting — including wire snares — as major threats. We do not lock a status letter.

questions.title: Sea to mountains
questions.stem: Across what kinds of forest can wild Sumatran tigers live?
choices: Only frozen ice fields
Only desert dunes
From coastal lowland forest up into high mountain forest
questions.why: Wikipedia says they range from sea-level coastal lowland forest to high mountain forest on Sumatra.

questions.title: Ambush hunter
questions.stem: How does a tiger usually catch its prey?
choices: It stalks and surprises them — an ambush, not a long open chase
It runs prey down over many miles like a long-distance racer
It waits for prey to climb into its mouth
questions.why: Wikipedia’s Tiger page says a tiger takes prey by ambush. It is not a long-distance runner and gives up if a chase goes too far.

questions.title: Big forest blocks
questions.stem: What kind of forest do Sumatran tigers need to thrive?
choices: Tiny backyard gardens
Large connected forest blocks — edges and broken scraps make life harder
Only one tree in the middle of a town
questions.why: Wikipedia says tigers need large contiguous forest blocks. Camera-trap work also shows they tend to avoid forest edges.

questions.title: Stripe-to-spot tips
questions.stem: What happens near the ends of a Sumatran tiger’s stripes?
choices: Each stripe turns into a rainbow
The stripes are painted on with a brush
Stripes often dissolve into spots, and small dark spots sit between the stripes
questions.why: Wikipedia says stripes tend to dissolve into spots near their ends, and lines of small dark spots sit between the regular stripes.

questions.title: Park strongholds
questions.stem: Where do the largest groups of wild Sumatran tigers live?
choices: In major national parks, which hold the biggest remaining groups
Only in backyard gardens
Scattered evenly on every city street
questions.why: Wikipedia says the largest remaining groups live in major national parks such as Kerinci Seblat and Gunung Leuser. We do not lock one head-count.

questions.title: Sondaica lumping
questions.stem: What did the 2017 Cat Specialist Group review do with living Sumatran tigers and the extinct Bali and Java tigers?
choices: It treats living Sumatran plus extinct Bali and Java tigers as Panthera tigris sondaica — though older sumatrae still appears
It proved they were three forever-separate species with no shared name
It renamed every tiger on Earth after a zoo nickname
questions.why: Wikipedia says the 2017 Cat Classification Task Force recognises living and extinct Indonesian tiger populations as P. t. sondaica. Pocock’s older name P. t. sumatrae still turns up in books and records. The lump is a taxonomic revision, not a claim that the island forms were identical in every trait.

questions.title: Status snapshot
questions.stem: How should we read a Critically Endangered letter for the Sumatran tiger?
choices: The letter is a forever grade that can never change
It is often listed Critically Endangered — a snapshot, not a forever letter
Scientists have declared it extinct in the wild
questions.why: Listings have often treated the Sumatran tiger as Critically Endangered. Status letters can be revised when new counts or methods arrive, so we treat CR as a snapshot, not a locked forever grade.

questions.title: Hundreds, not a census
questions.stem: About how many Sumatran tigers are thought to remain in the wild?
choices: Tens of millions, spread evenly across Asia
Exactly one pair left in a single zoo
On the order of hundreds, living in fragmented pockets — counts are estimates, not a locked census
questions.why: Wikipedia cites island-wide estimates in the hundreds and notes they persist in small, fragmented populations. Survey methods and years differ, so we do not lock one head-count.

questions.title: Plantation expansion
questions.stem: What is a major driver of Sumatran tiger forest loss?
choices: Expansion of oil palm and acacia plantations that replace forest
Too many birthday cakes in national parks
Tigers choosing to live only in cities
questions.why: Wikipedia names habitat loss from expanding palm-oil (oil palm) and acacia plantations as a major threat, along with prey decline and illegal trade. Hunting is real, but plantation expansion is a key forest-loss driver.

questions.title: Island isolation
questions.stem: How did Sumatran tigers become cut off from mainland tigers?
choices: A zoo boat moved them last year
After Ice Age seas rose, Sumatra was isolated from the mainland — dating of that rise is approximate
They always lived only on icebergs
questions.why: Wikipedia links isolation to a sea-level rise at the Pleistocene-to-Holocene transition after the last Ice Age. Exact thousand-year dates are debated, so we keep the timing soft. A vanished land bridge once connected island and mainland populations.

questions.title: Genetic isolation
questions.stem: What do mitochondrial DNA and microsatellite studies say about Sumatran tigers versus mainland tigers?
choices: They are genetically identical to every mainland tiger
They have no DNA at all
They are genetically isolated from living mainland tigers, with distinctive mtDNA and microsatellite markers
questions.why: Wikipedia says complete mitochondrial genes support a diagnostically distinct Sumatran form. Isolation from mainland tigers is backed by unique mitochondrial DNA sites and haplotypes plus unique microsatellite alleles. Mainland tigers form a closely related group of their own. We do not lock one marker count.

questions.title: Studbook bottleneck
questions.stem: What is a genetics worry in captive Sumatran tigers?
choices: The global studbook rests on few founders, and some cubs have shown inbreeding-linked vestibular (inner-ear) problems
They have thousands of unrelated wild founders and no inbreeding risk
Captive tigers never have medical records
questions.why: Wikipedia notes the global studbook traces captive Sumatran tigers to a small founder group. Some cubs have shown congenital vestibular trouble — ataxia, head tilt, and related signs — most likely linked to close relatedness and inbreeding. We do not lock one founder count.

questions.title: CITES Appendix I
questions.stem: How does international law treat trade in tigers, including the Sumatran tiger?
choices: Tiger parts can be sold freely in any shop
Panthera tigris is on CITES Appendix I, so international trade is tightly controlled
CITES only covers house cats
questions.why: Wikipedia says Panthera tigris is listed on CITES Appendix I. That listing tightly controls international commercial trade. Hunting is also prohibited in Indonesia. Appendix I is a trade rule, not the same thing as an IUCN status letter.

questions.title: Snares and bycatch
questions.stem: How do wire snares harm Sumatran tigers even when a hunter is not targeting a tiger?
choices: Snares only catch butterflies
Snares help tigers hunt more safely
Poachers set wire snares for tigers, and tigers are also caught by accident in traps meant for deer or wild pigs
questions.why: Wikipedia says poachers target tigers with wire snares, and tigers are also inadvertently caught in traps set by deer hunters and by farmers trying to stop wild-boar crop raids. Snares are a major mortality source — targeted and bycatch.

questions.title: Conflict edges
questions.stem: Where do people and Sumatran tigers most often come into conflict?
choices: Where forest meets farms and settlements — the busy edges
Only in the middle of the deepest untouched forest
Only on the open ocean
questions.why: Wikipedia names conflict with people as a major threat. Tigers use human-dominated landscapes at the fringes of protected areas less than core forest, but those edges — farms, settlements, and encroachment — are where encounters and retaliation killings cluster.

western-lowland-gorilla.source_note: Facts from Wikipedia, Western lowland gorilla.
talk_about: Why might a silverback lead a family instead of living alone?
If you could knuckle-walk, what would you notice first at the zoo?
Which other animal at the zoo lives in a family group?
push_further: A threat letter on a list can change. Why treat it as a snapshot, not a forever grade?
Gorillas eat plants and build a new nest each night. How is that different from a King Kong movie?
Find one more ape on your zoo map. How does it use its hands?

teach: Wild western lowland gorillas live in Central African forests — rainforest and swamp forest.
They eat mostly plants — fruit, leaves, stems, and bark — and sometimes insects.
A silverback is an adult male with a silver-grey back who leads the family.
A family troop is females and young living with the silverback.
They are the smallest kind of gorilla — and still huge.

questions.title: Central Africa forests
questions.stem: Where do wild western lowland gorillas live?
choices: Central African forests — rainforest and swamp forest
Only on frozen ice
Only in open desert
questions.why: Wikipedia says they live in forest and lowland swampland in central Africa — rainforest and swamp forest, not ice or desert.

questions.title: Mostly plants
questions.stem: What do western lowland gorillas mostly eat?
choices: Mostly meat like a lion
Mostly plants — fruit, leaves, stems, and bark
Only fish
questions.why: Wikipedia says they are primarily herbivorous — fruit, leaves, stems, and bark — and may eat insects from time to time.

questions.title: Silverback
questions.stem: What is a silverback?
choices: A baby gorilla with white socks
A gorilla painted silver at the zoo
An adult male with a silver-grey back who leads
questions.why: Wikipedia says older males get grey hair on the back and rump — that is why they are called silverbacks — and the silverback leads the group.

questions.title: Family troop
questions.stem: Who usually lives with a silverback?
choices: Females and their young
Only other silverbacks and no young
A huge pride of lions
questions.why: Wikipedia says breeding groups are one silverback, adult females, and their offspring. The male’s role is protector.

questions.title: Smallest gorilla
questions.stem: How does a western lowland gorilla’s size compare with other gorillas?
choices: It is as small as a house cat
It is the smallest kind of gorilla — and still huge
It is the only gorilla that can fly
questions.why: Wikipedia calls it the smallest of the four gorilla subspecies. We do not lock one weight.

questions.title: Knuckle-walk
questions.stem: How do western lowland gorillas usually walk on the ground?
choices: On two feet all day like people
Only by swinging and never touching the ground
On their knuckles, with hands curled on the ground
questions.why: Wikipedia says they walk in a hunched, four-legged way with hands curled and knuckles touching the ground.

questions.title: Display, not mean
questions.stem: What does a chest-beat or charge usually mean?
choices: It is a display of power — they are usually calm unless disturbed
They are always hunting people
They are trying to fly
questions.why: Wikipedia says a silverback may stand up, charge, and pound his chest, but gorillas are generally calm and nonaggressive unless they are disturbed.

questions.title: Baby rides
questions.stem: How do baby western lowland gorillas travel with mom?
choices: They fly on their own
They cling and ride on mom for years
They ride on elephants
questions.why: Wikipedia says infants cling to mom’s fur and ride on her back for years — not just a day.

questions.title: Night nests
questions.stem: Where do western lowland gorillas sleep at night?
choices: In the same permanent cave every year
Underwater like hippos
In leafy nests they make each night
questions.why: Wikipedia notes night nests — some in trees, many on the ground. They build leafy nests for the night.

questions.title: Myth buster — King Kong
questions.stem: Are western lowland gorillas movie monsters like King Kong?
choices: No — they are plant-eating family apes
Yes — they hunt cities for meat
They are robots
questions.why: Wikipedia describes plant-eating family groups led by a silverback — not movie monsters.

questions.title: Fruit when ripe
questions.stem: When do western lowland gorillas eat the most fruit?
choices: They eat more fruit when ripe fruit is available, and more leaves, stems, and bark when fruit is scarce
They eat only meat all year
They never eat plants
questions.why: Wikipedia says when ripe fruit is available they eat more fruit; when it is scarce they eat leaves, herbs, and bark.

questions.title: Swamp and clearings
questions.stem: Besides rainforest, which feeding places matter a lot for western lowland gorillas?
choices: Only city parks
Swamp forest and open forest clearings called bais
Only icy mountaintops
questions.why: Wikipedia says swamp forest is an important food source and habitat, and groups use large open clearings — swamps and bais — as they follow ripening fruit.

questions.title: Overlapping ranges
questions.stem: How do western lowland gorilla groups treat their home ranges?
choices: Each group owns a locked territory that no neighbor may enter
They migrate across the whole ocean
They are not strongly territorial — neighboring groups’ ranges often overlap
questions.why: Wikipedia says gorillas do not display territorial behavior, and neighboring groups often overlap ranges.

questions.title: Bachelor years
questions.stem: What happens after a young male leaves his birth group?
choices: He may spend years alone or with other males before leading a family
He instantly becomes the silverback of that same family
He turns into a chimpanzee
questions.why: Wikipedia says males leave their natal group before maturity and go through a bachelor stage that can last several years, alone or in a nonbreeding group.

questions.title: Size gap
questions.stem: How do male and female western lowland gorillas compare in size?
choices: Females are always much larger than males
Males are much larger than females — a big size gap
They are the same size as house cats
questions.why: Wikipedia says this subspecies shows pronounced sexual dimorphism — males are much larger than females. We do not lock one weight.

questions.title: Seed movers
questions.stem: How do western lowland gorillas help the forest grow new plants?
choices: They plant seeds with shovels
They burn the forest every night
They spread seeds in their dung as they travel
questions.why: Wikipedia says they are seed dispersers. Seeds pass through the gut and land in dung, which helps many forest plants.

questions.title: Threats
questions.stem: What puts wild western lowland gorillas under pressure today?
choices: Bushmeat hunting and forest loss
Too many birthday parties
They have no wild threats
questions.why: Wikipedia names hunting for bushmeat and habitat destruction from logging and expanding settlements. We do not lock a status letter.

questions.title: Zoo gorilla
questions.stem: Which gorilla do you almost always meet in a zoo?
choices: Almost every zoo gorilla is a mountain gorilla from the highlands
Nearly all zoo gorillas are western lowland gorillas
Zoos keep only movie-monster costumes
questions.why: Wikipedia says the western lowland gorilla is the subspecies almost always kept in zoos — nearly all zoo gorillas are this kind.

questions.title: Avoid people
questions.stem: How do wild western lowland gorillas usually treat villages, roads, and farms?
choices: They prefer to live in town centers
They build houses next to highways
They stay away from villages, roads, and farms that show people nearby
questions.why: Wikipedia says they are not typically seen near human settlements and villages, and they avoid roads and farms that show signs of human activity.

questions.title: Slow family
questions.stem: How fast do western lowland gorilla families grow?
choices: Families grow slowly — few young, and infants stay dependent for a long time
Females have huge litters every month
Babies live on their own from day one
questions.why: Wikipedia says females do not produce many offspring, and infants can stay dependent on mom for years. We keep the ages soft.

questions.title: Status snapshot
questions.stem: How should we read a Critically Endangered letter for the western lowland gorilla?
choices: It is often listed Critically Endangered after hunting and disease — a snapshot, not a forever letter
The letter is a forever grade that can never change
Scientists have declared it extinct in the wild
questions.why: Listings have often treated the western lowland gorilla as Critically Endangered, citing hunting and disease. Status letters can be revised when new counts or methods arrive, so we treat CR as a snapshot, not a locked forever grade.

questions.title: Ebola outbreaks
questions.stem: What has Ebola done to some wild western lowland gorilla groups?
choices: It only gives them a mild cold and never changes group size
It has caused catastrophic drops in some wild groups — exact percents and head-counts are contested
It made every gorilla on Earth extinct
questions.why: Wikipedia describes Ebola outbreaks emptying some Congo forest groups. Some write-ups cite very high mortality, but percents and head-counts differ by site and year, so we keep those numbers soft.

questions.title: SIV and HIV-1
questions.stem: How are western lowland gorilla SIVs linked to some HIV-1 lineages?
choices: Gorillas invented HIV in a lab last year
Gorillas have no viruses at all
Gorilla SIVs — simian immunodeficiency viruses — are related to some HIV-1 lineages that later infected people
questions.why: Wikipedia says western lowland gorillas are one likely zoonotic source of some HIV-1 lineages. The simian virus (SIV) in gorillas sits near certain HIV-1 groups on the family tree. That is a virus-history link — it does not mean a zoo gorilla has HIV or AIDS.

questions.title: Gorilla genome
questions.stem: What did sequencing the gorilla genome in 2012 show about humans and chimps?
choices: It was sequenced in 2012; some regions look closer to human than chimpanzee — exact percents are contested
Gorillas have no DNA and cannot be compared with people
It proved gorillas are more closely related to plants than to apes
questions.why: Wikipedia says the gorilla genome was sequenced in 2012. Some stretches look more like human than chimpanzee, a pattern called incomplete lineage sorting. Published percent shares differ by region and method, so we do not lock one number.

questions.title: Cross River cousin
questions.stem: How does the western lowland gorilla sit next to the Cross River gorilla?
choices: They are the same as mountain gorillas and have no cousins
Western gorillas include G. g. gorilla (western lowland) and G. g. diehli (Cross River)
Cross River gorillas live only in Antarctica
questions.why: Wikipedia treats the western lowland gorilla as Gorilla gorilla gorilla and names the Cross River gorilla, Gorilla gorilla diehli, as the other western gorilla subspecies.

questions.title: Snowflake genetics
questions.stem: What did genetics show about Snowflake, the albino western lowland gorilla?
choices: He was painted white at the zoo
All gorillas are albino
A change in SLC45A2 caused his albinism; related carrier parents gave evidence of inbreeding
questions.why: Wikipedia says Snowflake’s albinism came from a recessive change in SLC45A2. His parents were related carriers (an uncle and niece), which gave the first evidence of inbreeding in western lowland gorillas.

questions.title: Deep tool use
questions.stem: How have wild western lowland gorillas been seen using sticks as tools?
choices: They modify sticks to fit holes for food, and one was seen using a stick to gauge water depth
They only use metal hammers from hardware stores
They never touch sticks
questions.why: Wikipedia says they select branches, strip leaves or bark, and shorten sticks to fit food holes — starting with a bigger stick and shaping it. A gorilla has also been seen using a stick to measure water depth.

questions.title: Nominate subspecies
questions.stem: What does the scientific name Gorilla gorilla gorilla mean?
choices: It is a zoo nickname with no science meaning
It marks the nominate subspecies of the western gorilla
It means they are three different species living in the ocean
questions.why: Wikipedia calls the western lowland gorilla the nominate subspecies of the western gorilla — the form that carries the same name three times: Gorilla gorilla gorilla.

questions.title: Logging roads
questions.stem: How do logging roads put western lowland gorillas at extra risk?
choices: Roads plant extra fruit trees for gorillas
Roads scare all insects away and nothing else changes
They let hunters travel deeper into the forest, enabling more bushmeat hunting
questions.why: Wikipedia links commercial logging to new roads that let hunters go farther into the forest. Those roads raise poaching and the bushmeat trade, beyond the trees cut down.

questions.title: Swamp strongholds
questions.stem: Where do large remaining wild western lowland gorilla populations find shelter?
choices: Large Congo swamp forests shelter major populations
Only on icebergs
Only in city parks
questions.why: Wikipedia says isolated swampy forests in the Republic of the Congo hold a large share of the remaining wild animals. Later surveys found many more in those swamps. We do not lock one head-count.

talk_about: Cheetahs hunt in the day, while lions often hunt at night. How could that help them share the plains?
Lions and hyenas often steal a cheetah’s meal. How could a cheetah still get enough to eat?
A cheetah sneaks close before it sprints. Why not start the chase from far away?
push_further: Cheetah claws stay out more than a house cat’s. What would you ask a keeper about that?
Some brother cheetahs hunt together. Why might a team help on the plains?
Wild cheetahs can look very alike. What would you ask a keeper about telling them apart?

teach: They are the fastest animal on land — built for short sprints.
They have solid black spots, not the rosettes a leopard has.
Black tear marks run from each eye toward the nose.
They chirp and purr — they do not roar like a lion.
They live mostly on African grassland / savannah.

questions.title: Fastest on land
questions.stem: What is a cheetah famous for?
choices: Being the fastest animal on land
Being the slowest animal on land
Being the only animal that can fly
questions.why: Wikipedia calls the cheetah the fastest land animal. We do not lock one exact speed.

questions.title: Solid spots
questions.stem: What kind of marks does a cheetah’s coat have?
choices: Leopard-style rosettes with rings
Solid black spots — not leopard rosettes
No marks at all — a plain gold coat
questions.why: Wikipedia says a cheetah’s fur is marked with evenly spaced, solid black spots. A leopard has rosettes instead.

questions.title: Tear marks
questions.stem: What are the black lines on a cheetah’s face?
choices: Paint added at the zoo
Stripes that cover the whole body
Tear marks — black lines from each eye toward the nose
questions.why: Wikipedia describes black tear-like facial streaks from the corners of the eyes down the side of the nose.

questions.title: No roar
questions.stem: What sounds is a cheetah known for?
choices: Chirps and purrs — not a lion-like roar
A deep roar that shakes the whole savannah
A moo like a cow
questions.why: Wikipedia lists bird-like chirps and a loud purr. Cheetahs are not known for a lion-like roar.

questions.title: Savannah home
questions.stem: Where do most wild cheetahs live?
choices: Only on frozen ice
Mostly African grassland / savannah
Only deep under the ocean
questions.why: Wikipedia says cheetahs in eastern and southern Africa occur mostly in savannas. They seldom live in tropical forests.

questions.title: Sprint body
questions.stem: How is a cheetah’s body built for a chase?
choices: Short legs, a stiff back, and a heavy lion-like body
Wings and fins instead of legs
A slim body, long legs, and a flexible spine
questions.why: Wikipedia says the cheetah evolved for speed, with powerful hindlimb muscles, long limbs, and a flexible spine. Its slim form is built for running.

questions.title: Steering tail
questions.stem: How does a cheetah’s long tail help in a chase?
choices: It helps the cheetah balance and steer
It stores water like a camel hump
It is used to fly over the grass
questions.why: Wikipedia says the long tail works like a rudder. It helps the cheetah turn and stay balanced while chasing prey.

questions.title: Meat hunter
questions.stem: What do wild cheetahs mostly hunt?
choices: Only leaves and grass
Medium antelopes and gazelles
Only fish in deep rivers
questions.why: Wikipedia says cheetahs prefer medium-sized hooved animals such as impala, springbok, and Thomson’s gazelles.

questions.title: Cub cape
questions.stem: What special fur do cheetah cubs have on their backs?
choices: A hard shell like a tortoise
Bright blue feathers
A fluffy grey cape that helps them hide
questions.why: Wikipedia says a cub’s nape, shoulders, and back are thickly covered with long bluish-grey hair called a mantle. That fluffy cape can help the cub stay hidden.

questions.title: Myth buster — marathon
questions.stem: Do cheetahs run fast for a long time, like a marathon?
choices: No — they sprint in short bursts, not long runs
Yes — they jog for hours without stopping
They only hop slowly and never sprint
questions.why: Wikipedia describes short, high-speed chases — often under a minute — not long marathon runs. After a hunt, a cheetah needs to rest.

questions.title: Soft top speed
questions.stem: About how fast can a cheetah run in a short burst?
choices: Around 50–65 miles an hour — we do not lock one exact record
About as slow as a tortoise on land
Faster than a jet plane
questions.why: Wikipedia places a cheetah’s top speed in a band around 50–65 miles an hour. Famous one-number records have been questioned, so we do not lock an exact figure.

questions.title: Day hunter
questions.stem: When do wild cheetahs usually hunt?
choices: Only in the middle of the night, like many lions
Mostly in the day — that helps them avoid lions and hyenas
Only underwater
questions.why: Wikipedia says the cheetah is mainly active in the day, with peaks around dawn and dusk. Hunting by day helps it avoid larger, often night-active hunters like lions.

questions.title: Spine spring
questions.stem: How does a cheetah’s flexible spine help it run?
choices: It stores water like a camel
It keeps the cheetah from ever bending
It works like a spring and lengthens each stride
questions.why: Wikipedia says a flexible spine lets the body stretch and fold. That extra bend lengthens the stride so the cheetah covers more ground with each bound.

questions.title: Kill thieves
questions.stem: What often happens after a cheetah makes a kill?
choices: Larger hunters like lions or hyenas may steal the meal, so it eats fast
The cheetah always stores the meat in a tree for a week
Nothing — no other animal ever comes near
questions.why: Wikipedia says larger, stronger carnivores steal cheetah kills. Cheetahs often eat quickly and may drag the meal toward cover.

questions.title: Medium prey
questions.stem: What size of prey do wild cheetahs usually hunt?
choices: The biggest animals on the plains, like adult elephants
Medium gazelles and antelopes — not the biggest game
Only tiny insects
questions.why: Wikipedia says cheetahs prefer medium-sized hooved animals such as gazelles, impala, and springbok. They usually avoid the very largest game.

questions.title: Stalk then sprint
questions.stem: How does a cheetah usually start a hunt?
choices: It roars from far away to scare the herd
It waits in a river until prey swims by
It stalks close first, then sprints
questions.why: Wikipedia says a cheetah typically stalks and closes in — often to a few dozen or a couple of hundred metres — before the high-speed charge.

questions.title: Cub danger
questions.stem: What is a big danger for wild cheetah cubs?
choices: Lions and hyenas — cubs are highly vulnerable to those hunters
They are never in danger from other animals
They only have to worry about falling from trees
questions.why: Wikipedia says cheetah cubs are highly vulnerable to predators. Lions and hyenas are a main reason many cubs do not survive.

questions.title: Threats
questions.stem: What puts wild cheetahs under pressure today?
choices: Too many trees on the moon
Habitat loss and conflict with people
An extra-long winter every year
questions.why: Wikipedia lists habitat loss and conflict with people among the main threats. We do not lock a status letter — that grade is a snapshot and can change.

questions.title: Spot fingerprint
questions.stem: What is special about a cheetah’s spot pattern?
choices: Every cheetah has the exact same spots
The spots are painted on at the zoo
Each cheetah’s spots are unique, like a fingerprint
questions.why: Wikipedia says each cheetah has a distinct spot pattern that can be used to tell individuals apart.

questions.title: Short chase
questions.stem: How long is a typical cheetah chase?
choices: A brief burst over a few hundred metres — not a long run
Many miles, like a marathon
It never runs at all
questions.why: Wikipedia describes short, high-speed chases. Studies find an average chase of a few hundred metres — often under a minute — not a long run.
